Chapter 12: Monetary Policy and the Phillips Curve

Learning goals

Chapter 11 built the IS curve, which links the real interest rate to short-run output. This chapter adds the two missing pieces of the short-run model: the MP curve (how the central bank sets the real interest rate) and the Phillips curve (how output moves inflation over time). By the end of it you will be able to:

  • explain why a central bank that sets a nominal interest rate also sets the real interest rate in the short run, using the Fisher equation and the assumption of sticky inflation;
  • use the IS/MP diagram to analyze monetary policy and demand shocks, such as the end of a housing bubble;
  • explain the Phillips curve \(\Delta\pi_t = \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t + \bar{o}\), with adaptive expectations and price shocks;
  • simulate the Volcker disinflation year by year and explain how mistakes contributed to the Great Inflation;
  • read U.S. data on the federal funds rate, the yield curve, inflation and the Covid-19 recession, and compare them with dozens of other countries;
  • in Python: draw several panels with make_subplots, simulate a model with a loop, reshape tables with melt and pivot, join tables with merge, animate a chart with animation_frame, and fit a trend with np.polyfit.

# @title Helper for the website versions (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def slider_figure(make_figure, name, values, start, label=None):
    """Precompute make_figure(name=value) for every value and join the results with one slider.

    The website cannot run Python, so each interactive figure also gets this precomputed version.
    """
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    first = values.index(start)
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[first].layout)
    owner = []                                  # which precomputed figure each trace comes from
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (i == first)
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    steps = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(),
                  "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations],
                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes]}
        visible = [o == i for o in owner]
        steps.append(dict(method="update", label=str(values[i]), args=[{"visible": visible}, layout]))
    fig.update_layout(sliders=[dict(active=first, steps=steps, pad=dict(t=60),
                                    currentvalue=dict(prefix=(label or name) + " = "))])
    return fig

Model overview

This chapter completes the short-run model. It explains how the central bank moves the economy and how the economy, in turn, moves inflation. The chain has three links. The central bank sets a nominal interest rate, and because inflation adjusts slowly, it also sets the real interest rate (the MP curve). The real interest rate sets short-run output through the IS curve of Chapter 11. And short-run output changes inflation over time through the Phillips curve: a booming economy pushes inflation up, a slump pulls it down.

The inputs are the central bank’s interest rate and the shocks that hit the economy, to demand or to prices; the outcomes are short-run output and inflation, period by period. Below we write the three equations, fix one baseline for every diagram, and define the functions that the sections reuse: the IS/MP diagram, the Phillips curve, a year-by-year simulation of the whole model, the money market, and the tools for comparing countries in the data figures.

The short-run model has three building blocks. Each one links two variables, and together they form a chain from the central bank’s interest rate to inflation.

1. The MP curve. The central bank sets a short-term nominal interest rate \(i_t\). The Fisher equation links it to the real interest rate \(R_t\) and the inflation rate \(\pi_t\):

\[i_t = R_t + \pi_t \qquad (12.1) \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad R_t = i_t - \pi_t. \qquad (12.2)\]

The key assumption is sticky inflation: in the very short run (say six months), inflation does not react to monetary policy. So when the central bank moves \(i_t\), \(R_t\) moves one for one. In effect the central bank chooses the real interest rate, and the MP curve is a horizontal line at that rate.

2. The IS curve of Chapter 11 turns the real interest rate into short-run output:

\[\tilde{Y}_t = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\,(R_t - \bar{r}). \qquad (11.12)\]

3. The Phillips curve. Firms raise their prices by the inflation they expect, plus an adjustment for demand. With adaptive expectations, \(\pi^e_t = \pi_{t-1}\), and with a price shock \(\bar{o}\) (an oil shock, for example):

\[\pi_t = \pi_{t-1} + \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t + \bar{o} \qquad (12.7) \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \Delta\pi_t = \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t + \bar{o}. \qquad (12.8)\]

One baseline for every diagram. The textbook draws its diagrams without numbers, apart from a few examples. All the figures of this notebook start from one set of values:

  • the IS curve of Chapter 11’s numerical example: no demand shock \(\bar{a} = 0\), \(\bar{b} = 2\) and a marginal product of capital \(\bar{r} = 5\) percent. Then the textbook’s “\(-2\) percent” in Figs. 12.4, 12.5 and 12.10 comes from \(R' = 6\) percent or from \(\bar{a}' = -2\);
  • the slope of the Phillips curve \(\bar{\nu} = 0.5\) (illustrative; Chapter 9 estimated about 1/3 for the United States) and no price shock, \(\bar{o} = 0\);
  • sticky inflation of 2 percent in normal times and 10 percent at the start of the Volcker disinflation (the textbook’s number);
  • a money market with money demand \(M^d = 10 - i\) and money supply \(\bar{M}^s = 5\) (illustrative units), so that the nominal interest rate is 5 percent;
  • for the productivity slowdown of Fig. 13, potential output growth of 3.5 percent a year before 1973 and 2.5 percent after (illustrative).

Python note. def creates a function: a named recipe that takes inputs (the arguments) and gives back a result with return. Writing b=B_BAR gives the argument a default value, used whenever we do not pass one; here the default is a constant we defined just before. The text in triple quotes is a short description of what the function does.

A_BAR, B_BAR, R_BAR = 0.0, 2.0, 5.0     # IS curve: no demand shock, b = 2, r_bar = 5 percent
NU, O_BAR = 0.5, 0.0                     # Phillips curve: slope nu = 0.5, no price shock
M0, M_BAR = 10.0, 5.0                    # money market: demand M = 10 - i, supply 5 (units)


def real_rate(i, pi):
    """Equation 12.2, the Fisher equation: the real interest rate R = i - pi, in percent."""
    return i - pi


def is_curve(R, a=A_BAR, b=B_BAR, r_bar=R_BAR):
    """Equation 11.12, the IS curve: short-run output Y~ = a - b (R - r_bar), in percent."""
    return a - b * (R - r_bar)


def rate_for_output(Y, a=A_BAR, b=B_BAR, r_bar=R_BAR):
    """The IS curve solved for R: the real interest rate at which short-run output equals Y."""
    return r_bar + (a - Y) / b


def phillips(Y, nu=NU, o=O_BAR):
    """Equation 12.8, the Phillips curve: the change in inflation = nu * Y~ + o, in percentage points."""
    return nu * Y + o

The money market of Section 12.7 has two more functions. People hold less money when the nominal interest rate, the opportunity cost of holding money, is higher.

def money_demand(i, m0=M0):
    """Fig. 12.18: money demanded falls as the nominal interest rate rises, M = m0 - i."""
    return m0 - i


def market_rate(M_s, m0=M0):
    """The nominal rate that clears the money market: m0 - i = M_s, so i = m0 - M_s."""
    return m0 - M_s

The full model runs year by year: the central bank sets \(R_t\), the IS curve gives \(\tilde{Y}_t\), and the Phillips curve turns last year’s inflation into this year’s. simulate repeats these three steps for a whole path of interest rates.

Python note. A for loop repeats the indented lines once for each number in R_path. Y_path = [] starts an empty list, and .append(...) adds one number at its end. np.array(...) turns a list into an array, so that we can do arithmetic with it.

def simulate(R_path, pi_start, nu=NU, a=A_BAR):
    """The short-run model year by year: MP sets R, IS gives Y~, the Phillips curve gives pi (eq. 12.7)."""
    Y_path, pi_path = [], []
    pi = pi_start                          # inflation of the year before the first year
    for R in R_path:
        Y = is_curve(R, a)
        pi = pi + phillips(Y, nu)          # last year's inflation, adjusted for demand
        Y_path.append(Y)
        pi_path.append(pi)
    return np.array(Y_path), np.array(pi_path)

Let us try the functions on the textbook’s examples.

Python note. An f-string such as f"R = {value:.1f}%" inserts the value of a variable into a piece of text; :.1f means “show one decimal” and :+.2f “show the sign and two decimals”.

print(f"Fisher: i = 7%, pi = 2%    ->  R = {real_rate(7.0, 2.0):.1f}%")
print(f"IS: R = 5%  ->  Y~ = {is_curve(5.0):+.1f}%;   R = 6%  ->  Y~ = {is_curve(6.0):+.1f}%")
print(f"Housing bust a' = -2: the rate that keeps Y~ = 0 is R' = {rate_for_output(0.0, a=-2.0):.1f}%")
print(f"Phillips curve: Y~ = -2%  ->  change in inflation {phillips(-2.0):+.2f} points")
print(f"Oil shock o = 1 at Y~ = 0  ->  change in inflation {phillips(0.0, o=1.0):+.2f} points")
print(f"Money market: supply 5  ->  i = {market_rate(5.0):.1f}%;   supply 4  ->  i = {market_rate(4.0):.1f}%")
Y_path, pi_path = simulate([6.0, 6.0, 6.0, 6.0, 6.0, 5.0], pi_start=10.0)
print("Volcker: five years at R = 6%, then R = 5%. Inflation:", pi_path)
Fisher: i = 7%, pi = 2%    ->  R = 5.0%
IS: R = 5%  ->  Y~ = +0.0%;   R = 6%  ->  Y~ = -2.0%
Housing bust a' = -2: the rate that keeps Y~ = 0 is R' = 4.0%
Phillips curve: Y~ = -2%  ->  change in inflation -1.00 points
Oil shock o = 1 at Y~ = 0  ->  change in inflation +1.00 points
Money market: supply 5  ->  i = 5.0%;   supply 4  ->  i = 6.0%
Volcker: five years at R = 6%, then R = 5%. Inflation: [9. 8. 7. 6. 5. 5.]

Raising the real interest rate from 5 to 6 percent pushes output 2 percent below potential, as in the textbook. With \(\bar{\nu} = 0.5\), a 2 percent recession lowers inflation by 1 point a year, so five years of it bring inflation from 10 down to 5 percent, and it stays there once the interest rate is back at \(\bar{r}\).

Drawing tools

All the diagrams of this chapter are built from the same few pieces, so we write them once:

  • add_line draws a curve through some points and writes its label at the right end, as the textbook does. When an older curve of the same panel ends within 0.6 axis units, its label is removed, so that two labels never overlap;
  • add_is, add_pc and add_demand draw an IS curve, a Phillips curve and a money demand curve inside the fixed axes;
  • add_point marks a point with dashed guides to the axes and writes its label at the top right, or wherever where says, and add_arrow draws an arrow;
  • set_axes sets fixed axes, so that you can see the curves move when you change a slider.

Every function takes row and col arguments, so it can draw in one panel of a figure with several panels.

Python note. go.Figure() starts an empty chart and add_trace adds a line or a set of points. [""] * 3 is the list ["", "", ""], and + [label] adds one more element, so only the last point of a curve gets the label. fig.data[-1] is the trace just added and fig.data[:-1] all the earlier ones. max(a, b) and min(a, b) give the larger and the smaller of two numbers, and abs(x) the size of x without its sign. != means “is not equal to”.

def add_line(fig, x, y, label, color, dash="solid", row=None, col=None):
    """Draw a curve through the points (x, y) and write its label at the right end."""
    text = [""] * (len(x) - 1) + [label]
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=x, y=y, mode="lines+text", text=text, textposition="middle right",
                             textfont=dict(size=15, color=color), cliponaxis=False, showlegend=False,
                             line=dict(color=color, width=4, dash=dash)), row=row, col=col)
    new = fig.data[-1]
    for old in fig.data[:-1]:                  # an older curve of the same panel ending close by loses its label
        close = abs(old.x[-1] - new.x[-1]) < 0.6 and abs(old.y[-1] - new.y[-1]) < 0.6
        if old.mode == "lines+text" and old.xaxis == new.xaxis and close:
            old.text = None
def add_point(fig, x, y, label, x0, y0, row=None, col=None, where="top right"):
    """Mark the point (x, y) with a dot, a label (at `where`) and dashed guides to the axes, which start at (x0, y0)."""
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[x0, x, x], y=[y, y, y0], mode="lines", showlegend=False, hoverinfo="skip",
                             line=dict(color="black", width=1, dash="dash")), row=row, col=col)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[x], y=[y], mode="markers+text", text=[label], textposition=where,
                             textfont=dict(size=16), showlegend=False, marker=dict(color="black", size=12)),
                  row=row, col=col)


def add_arrow(fig, x0, y0, x1, y1, row=None, col=None):
    """Draw an arrow from (x0, y0) to (x1, y1); nothing if the two points are the same."""
    if (x0, y0) != (x1, y1):
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[x0, x1], y=[y0, y1], mode="lines+markers", showlegend=False, hoverinfo="skip",
                                 line=dict(color="black", width=2),
                                 marker=dict(symbol="arrow", size=[0, 14], angleref="previous", color="black")),
                      row=row, col=col)
def add_is(fig, label, color, a=A_BAR, b=B_BAR, dash="solid", row=None, col=None):
    """Draw the IS curve inside the axes (R between 1 and 9.5 percent, Y~ between -7 and 6)."""
    Y = np.array([max(-7.0, is_curve(9.5, a, b)), min(6.0, is_curve(1.0, a, b))])
    add_line(fig, Y, rate_for_output(Y, a, b), label, color, dash, row, col)


def add_pc(fig, label, color, nu=NU, o=O_BAR, dash="solid", row=None, col=None, top=4.0):
    """Draw the Phillips curve inside the axes from -top to top (change in inflation from 0.4 - top to top - 0.6)."""
    Y = np.array([max(-7.0, (0.4 - top - o) / nu), min(6.0, (top - 0.6 - o) / nu)])
    add_line(fig, Y, phillips(Y, nu, o), label, color, dash, row, col)


def add_demand(fig, label, color, m0=M0, dash="solid"):
    """Draw the money demand curve M = m0 - i for nominal rates from 9 (or m0, if lower) down to 1 percent."""
    i = np.array([min(9.0, m0), 1.0])
    add_line(fig, money_demand(i, m0), i, label, color, dash)


def set_axes(fig, xaxis, yaxis, row=None, col=None):
    """Fixed axes (title, range, ticks), so that you can see the curves move."""
    fig.update_xaxes(xaxis, row=row, col=col)
    fig.update_yaxes(yaxis, row=row, col=col)

The three kinds of diagram use these axes. The lowest tick of each axis is left out, so that no two numbers crowd the bottom-left corner. The Phillips curve diagram switches to the wider Y_DPI_WIDE only when a large shock and a steep curve would push the economy off the usual axis.

Python note. dict(title=..., range=...) is a dictionary: a set of named settings. We store the settings of each axis once and hand them to set_axes.

X_OUTPUT = dict(title="Short-run output, Ỹ (%)", range=[-8, 8], tickvals=[-6, -4, -2, 0, 2, 4, 6], zeroline=False)
Y_RATE = dict(title="Real interest rate, R (%)", range=[0, 10], tickvals=[2, 4, 6, 8], zeroline=False)
Y_DPI = dict(title="Change in inflation, Δπ", range=[-4, 4], tickvals=[-3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3], zeroline=False)
Y_DPI_WIDE = dict(Y_DPI, range=[-7, 7], tickvals=[-6, -4, -2, 0, 2, 4, 6])   # for large shocks and steep curves
X_MONEY = dict(title="Money, M", range=[0, 12], tickvals=[2, 4, 6, 8, 10], zeroline=False)
Y_NOMINAL = dict(title="Nominal interest rate, i (%)", range=[0, 10], tickvals=[2, 4, 6, 8], zeroline=False)
MP_X = [-8, 6.5]                         # the MP line runs across the diagram, leaving room for its label

Shading recessions

Six data figures shade the U.S. recessions, as dated by the National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER). The file recessions.csv lists, for each recession since 1953, the peak (the last month before the recession) and the trough (its last month).

Python note. pd.read_csv reads a data file into a DataFrame, a table with named columns, and parse_dates=[...] turns text such as "2007-12-01" into real dates. zip(recessions.peak, recessions.trough) hands over one (peak, trough) pair at a time, and fig.add_vrect shades the band between two dates.

recessions = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "recessions.csv", parse_dates=["peak", "trough"])


def shade_recessions(fig, start):
    """Shade every NBER recession that ends after the date `start` (Figs. 2, 9, 14-17)."""
    for peak, trough in zip(recessions.peak, recessions.trough):
        if trough >= pd.Timestamp(start):
            fig.add_vrect(x0=peak, x1=trough, fillcolor=BLUE, opacity=0.12, line_width=0)
    return fig

Countries and colors

Every data figure of this chapter can go beyond the United States: the same series exist for many other countries. The file countries.csv lists every economy in the chapter’s multi-country files, with its region and whether it belongs to the OECD. We give each country a fixed color, so that it keeps its color when you add or remove others. The textbook’s economies keep the chapter’s own colors.

countries = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "countries.csv")
BOOK_COLORS = {"United States": BLUE, "United Kingdom": TEAL, "Euro area": GREEN, "Japan": "#5aa0d8"}
G7 = ["Canada", "France", "Germany", "Italy", "Japan", "United Kingdom", "United States"]

The website shows the countries of a figure in groups: the G7, or one region. Two countries of the same group should never share a color. The colors come from a small tool; its palette has 44 colors: Plotly’s 24 dark ones, and the 20 darker ones of its 26 “Alphabet” colors.

Python note. PALETTE = [] starts an empty list, and .append adds one color at a time. In first_free, return inside a loop stops the function at the first color that fits, used.count(c) counts how often c appears in the list used, and reversed(PALETTE) walks through the palette from its last color.

LIGHT = ["#F7E1A0", "#E2E2E2", "#FBE426", "#16FF32", "#1CFFCE", "#2ED9FF"]   # too pale on white
PALETTE = []
for c in px.colors.qualitative.Dark24:                                       # 24 dark colors ...
    if c != "#2E91E5":
        PALETTE.append(c)
for c in px.colors.qualitative.Alphabet:
    if c not in LIGHT:
        PALETTE.append(c)                                                     # ... and 20 more: 44 in all
PALETTE.append("#2E91E5")                    # a medium blue, too close to the U.S. navy: used last


def first_free(used, taken):
    """The palette color least used in `used` (the group-mates' colors), preferring one no country has `taken` yet."""
    for c in PALETTE:
        if c not in used and c not in taken:
            return c
    best = PALETTE[-1]
    for c in reversed(PALETTE):                  # from the end, far from the colors always on show
        if used.count(c) < used.count(best):
            best = c                             # a big group shares out the colors evenly
    return best

Python note. group_colors walks through the countries one by one. dict(fixed or {}) starts from a copy of the fixed colors (an empty dictionary when there are none), continue skips a country that already has a color, and used collects the colors of the countries that are shown together with this one.

def group_colors(names, groups, fixed=None):
    """Give each country a color that no other country in its groups uses, as far as the palette allows.

    names: every country; groups: the lists of countries shown together (menu views); fixed: {country: color}
    for the textbook's countries, so the default view keeps the book's colors."""
    colors = dict(fixed or {})
    for name in names:
        if name in colors:
            continue
        used = []
        for group in groups:
            if name in group:
                for other in group:
                    if other in colors:
                        used.append(colors[other])
        colors[name] = first_free(used, list(colors.values()))
    return colors

Each multi-country figure gets its own colors from menu_colors, with the groups of its website menu.

Python note. countries.country[countries.region == region] keeps the names of one region’s countries, and list(...) turns them into a plain list.

def menu_colors(names):
    """Colors for one figure: no two countries of a website group (the G7, a region, all 40 or fewer) share one."""
    groups = [G7]
    for region in countries.region.unique():
        groups.append(list(countries.country[countries.region == region]))
    if len(names) <= 40:
        groups.append(list(names))                     # a short legend lists every country at once
    return group_colors(names, groups, BOOK_COLORS)

The website versions of the multi-country figures need two more helpers: a menu that switches between countries, and buttons that list one group of countries in the legend. Run the two cells and move on.

Show the helper code 
# @title Helpers for the website country menus (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def compact(fig):
    """Shrink a website figure (short dates, 4 significant digits, a short hover), so the saved notebook stays small."""
    for trace in fig.data:
        x = pd.Series(trace.x if trace.x is not None else [], dtype=object).infer_objects()
        if pd.api.types.is_datetime64_any_dtype(x):
            trace.x = x.dt.strftime("%Y-%m-%d").tolist()
        if trace.y is not None and np.asarray(trace.y).dtype.kind == "f":
            trace.y = [float(f"{v:.4g}") for v in trace.y]
        if "lines" in (trace.mode or "") and trace.hovertext is None:
            trace.hovertemplate = "%{fullData.name}<br>%{x}: %{y}<extra></extra>"
    return fig


def menu_figure(make_figure, name, values, start):
    """Precompute make_figure(name=value) for every value and join the results with one dropdown menu."""
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    first = values.index(start)
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[first].layout)
    owner, shown = [], []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            shown.append(True if trace.visible is None else trace.visible)
            trace.visible = shown[-1] if i == first else False
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    buttons = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(), "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations],
                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes], "legend.title.text": f.layout.legend.title.text,
                  "xaxis.range": f.layout.xaxis.range, "yaxis.range": f.layout.yaxis.range}
        visible = [shown[j] if o == i else False for j, o in enumerate(owner)]
        buttons.append(dict(label=str(values[i]), method="update", args=[{"visible": visible}, layout]))
    fig.update_layout(margin=dict(t=110), updatemenus=[dict(type="dropdown", buttons=buttons, active=first, x=0, y=1.02,
                                                            xanchor="left", yanchor="bottom")])   # above the plot
    return compact(fig)
Show the helper code 
# @title Helper for the website group buttons (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def group_menu(fig, book, small=8):
    """Buttons that list one group of countries in the legend (a small group is drawn at once); `book` is always drawn."""
    names = [t.name for t in fig.data]
    short = {"Europe and Central Asia": "Europe", "Asia and Pacific": "Asia-Pacific", "Middle East and Africa": "Africa, Mideast"}
    groups = {"Textbook": list(book), "G7": G7, "Americas": [], "Europe": [], "Asia-Pacific": [], "Africa, Mideast": []}
    for c, r in zip(countries.country, countries.region):
        if c in names:
            groups[short.get(r, r)].append(c)
    first = ["legendonly" if len(names) <= 40 else False] * len(names)   # a short legend lists every country
    buttons = []
    for label, members in groups.items():
        if not set(members) & set(names):
            continue                                   # no country of this group in the figure
        visible = []
        for j, n in enumerate(names):
            if n in book:
                visible.append(True)
            elif n in members:
                visible.append(True if len(members) <= small else "legendonly")
            else:
                visible.append(first[j] if label == "Textbook" else False)
        buttons.append(dict(label=label, method="restyle", args=[{"visible": visible}]))
    for trace, v in zip(fig.data, buttons[0]["args"][0]["visible"]):
        trace.visible = v
    fig.update_layout(margin=dict(t=120), updatemenus=list(fig.layout.updatemenus) + [dict(
        type="buttons", direction="right", x=0, y=1.02, xanchor="left", yanchor="bottom", buttons=buttons)])
    return compact(fig)

The short-run model at a glance

Before the details, a small live version of the whole chain: from the interest rate to output to inflation.

Fig. 1: The structure of the short-run model

Goal. See the whole short-run model at once: how the central bank’s nominal interest rate ends up changing inflation.

The textbook’s Fig. 12.1 is a chain of four circles. Each arrow is one building block:

\[i_t \;\xrightarrow{\text{MP curve}}\; R_t \;\xrightarrow{\text{IS curve}}\; \tilde{Y}_t \;\xrightarrow{\text{Phillips curve}}\; \Delta\pi_t\]

Here the chain is live. You choose the inputs: the nominal interest rate \(i\) that the central bank sets, the current (sticky) inflation rate \(\pi\), and the demand shock \(\bar{a}\). The circles show the outcomes that the model computes: the real interest rate, short-run output and the change in inflation. The baseline is normal times: inflation of 2 percent and a nominal rate of 7 percent, so that \(R = 5\% = \bar{r}\) and output is at potential.

Python note. fig.add_shape(type="circle", ...) draws a circle inside the box from (x0, y0) to (x1, y1), and add_annotation(..., showarrow=False) writes text at a point. for k in range(4): repeats the indented lines for k = 0, 1, 2, 3, so names[k] picks one name at a time. scaleanchor="x" gives both axes the same scale, so the circles stay round, and visible=False hides the axes.

def short_run_model(i=7.0, pi=2.0, a=0.0):
    """Fig. 12.1: the nominal rate sets R (MP), R sets Y~ (IS), and Y~ sets the change in inflation (PC)."""
    R = real_rate(i, pi)
    Y = is_curve(R, a)
    dpi = phillips(Y)
    names = ["Nominal<br>interest rate, i", "Real interest<br>rate, R", "Short-run<br>output, Ỹ", "Change in<br>inflation, Δπ"]
    values = [f"{i:.1f}%", f"{R:.1f}%", f"{Y:+.1f}%", f"{dpi:+.2f}"]
    links = ["MP<br>curve", "IS<br>curve", "Phillips<br>curve"]
    fig = go.Figure()
    for k in range(4):
        fig.add_shape(type="circle", x0=3.4 * k - 1.15, x1=3.4 * k + 1.15, y0=-1.15, y1=1.15,
                      line=dict(color=TEAL, width=3), fillcolor="#e6f5f1")
        fig.add_annotation(x=3.4 * k, y=0.35, text=names[k], showarrow=False, font=dict(size=12))
        fig.add_annotation(x=3.4 * k, y=-0.45, text=f"<b>{values[k]}</b>", showarrow=False, font=dict(size=20, color=BLUE))
    for k in range(3):
        add_arrow(fig, 3.4 * k + 1.2, 0.0, 3.4 * k + 2.2, 0.0)
        fig.add_annotation(x=3.4 * k + 1.7, y=0.5, text=links[k], showarrow=False, font=dict(size=12))
    fig.add_annotation(x=5.1, y=-1.7, showarrow=False, font=dict(size=14),
                       text=f"Inflation next year: {pi:.2f}% + ({dpi:+.2f}) = {pi + dpi:.2f}%")
    fig.update_xaxes(visible=False, range=[-1.5, 11.7])
    fig.update_yaxes(visible=False, range=[-2.2, 1.8], scaleanchor="x")
    fig.update_layout(title=f"i = {i:.1f}%, π = {pi:.1f}%  →  R = {R:.1f}%  →  Ỹ = {Y:+.1f}%  →  Δπ = {dpi:+.2f}")
    return fig

Python note. interact turns each argument of a function into a slider and calls the function again every time you move one. The ; at the end only hides an extra line of text.

interact(short_run_model,
         i=FloatSlider(value=7.0, min=2.0, max=12.0, step=0.5, description="nominal interest rate i (%)", style=WIDE),
         pi=FloatSlider(value=2.0, min=0.0, max=8.0, step=0.5, description="sticky inflation π (%)", style=WIDE),
         a=FloatSlider(value=0.0, min=-4.0, max=4.0, step=0.5, description="demand shock ā", style=WIDE));
Show the code of the website version 
# @title Website version: Fig. 1 with a precomputed slider for the nominal interest rate
slider_figure(short_run_model, "i", [5.0, 6.0, 7.0, 8.0, 9.0], start=7.0, label="nominal interest rate i (%)")

Source. Adapted from Fig. 12.1 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

What to notice.

  • Raise \(i\) from 7 to 8 percent with inflation stuck at 2 percent: \(R\) rises to 6 percent, output falls to \(-2\) percent, and inflation starts to fall by 1 point a year. This is the textbook’s summary of the model “in a nutshell”: \(\uparrow i \Rightarrow \uparrow R \Rightarrow \downarrow \tilde{Y} \Rightarrow \downarrow \Delta\pi\).
  • What matters is \(i - \pi\). Raise inflation and the nominal rate by the same amount: nothing real changes.
  • A negative demand shock lowers output at any interest rate; the central bank can offset it by cutting \(i\).

Your turn. Inflation is stuck at 4 percent and there is no demand shock. What nominal interest rate keeps the economy at potential? Find it with the sliders, then check it with real_rate and is_curve.

Hint

Output is at potential when \(R = \bar{r} = 5\) percent, so you need \(i - 4 = 5\). Try is_curve(real_rate(9.0, 4.0)).

The MP curve and the IS/MP diagram

The central bank sets the interest rate, and the IS/MP diagram shows what that does to output. We look at the fed funds rate, a rate hike, a housing bust and the yield curve.

Fig. 2: The federal funds rate

Goal. See how much the Federal Reserve’s main policy rate has moved since 1960, and compare it with other central banks.

The federal funds rate is the interest rate that banks charge each other for overnight loans. The Fed controls it because it stands ready to lend and borrow at a stated rate: no bank pays more than the Fed charges, and no bank lends for less than the Fed pays, or others would borrow cheaply and lend back at the higher rate (an arbitrage opportunity).

fedfunds = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig12-2.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
fedfunds.tail()
date fedfunds
796 2026-05-01 3.63
797 2026-06-01 3.63
798 2026-07-01 3.63
799 2026-08-01 3.63
800 2026-09-01 3.75

Each row is a month. fedfunds is the effective federal funds rate in percent, the average of the daily rates of that month. Let us find the highest and the lowest values.

Python note. .idxmax() gives the row label of the largest value, and .loc[row] picks that row. fedfunds.date.dt.year is the year of each date, and .between(2009, 2015) is true for the years from 2009 to 2015.

peak = fedfunds.loc[fedfunds.fedfunds.idxmax()]
latest = fedfunds.iloc[-1]                                  # the last row
zero_years = fedfunds[fedfunds.date.dt.year.between(2009, 2015)]
print(f"Highest: {peak.fedfunds:.2f}% in {peak.date:%B %Y}")
print(f"2009-2015: between {zero_years.fedfunds.min():.2f}% and {zero_years.fedfunds.max():.2f}%")
print(f"Latest: {latest.fedfunds:.2f}% in {latest.date:%B %Y}")
Highest: 19.10% in June 1981
2009-2015: between 0.07% and 0.24%
Latest: 3.75% in September 2026

Other central banks

Every central bank has a policy rate. The Bank for International Settlements (BIS) collects them for 49 central banks, and the file policy_rates_monthly.csv has one row per country and month. For the United States it repeats the monthly fed funds rate above; for the other countries it is the rate on the last day of each month.

Python note. groupby("country") makes one group of rows per country, and .date.agg(["min", "max"]) gives the first and the last date of each group. Comparing the column "max" with a date keeps the series that stop early.

rates = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "policy_rates_monthly.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
POLICY_COLORS = menu_colors(sorted(rates.country.unique()))
coverage = rates.groupby("country").date.agg(["min", "max"])
coverage[coverage["max"] < "2026-01-01"]                  # series that stop early

Look at your data. Eleven series stop early. Germany, France, Italy, Spain and four other countries handed their monetary policy to the European Central Bank in 1999 (Greece in 2001): after that, look at the Euro area. Croatia’s series ends in 2022, just before it joined the euro, and Argentina’s in mid-2025. Two more warnings: the euro-area series switches in September 2024 from the ECB’s main refinancing rate to its deposit rate (the ECB’s new steering rate), and in a few hyperinflations policy rates reached hundreds or even thousands of percent (Brazil around 1990). The chart says so in its title when a line leaves the chart.

The chart can zoom in on three episodes of this chapter: choose one from the menu. You can also add other countries.

Python note. rates.country.isin(countries) is true for the rows of the chosen countries, and .between(a, b) keeps the dates of the period. color="country" draws one line per country, and color_discrete_map=POLICY_COLORS (made by menu_colors when we read the file) gives each its fixed color. The loop for step in [20, 40, 80] raises the top of the axis in steps, only when a chosen country needs it. ", ".join(names) glues a list of names into one text. A SelectMultiple is a list in which you can pick several entries (hold Ctrl, or Cmd on a Mac, and click); the function receives the chosen names as a tuple.

PERIODS = {"1960–2026, all the data": (["1959-06-01", "2027-01-01"], [-1.5, 20]),   # 0 clear of the corner
           "The Volcker years, 1977–1987": (["1977-01-01", "1987-12-31"], [-0.8, 20]),
           "Near-zero rates after 2008, 2006–2016": (["2006-01-01", "2016-12-31"], [-0.8, 8]),
           "Covid-19 and after, 2019–2026": (["2019-01-01", "2026-12-31"], [-0.8, 8])}


def missing_or_off(part, column, countries, low, high):
    """Title text naming the chosen countries with no data in `part`, and those whose values leave [low, high]."""
    missing, off = [], []
    for name in countries:
        values = part[column][part.country == name]
        if values.empty:
            missing.append(name)
        elif values.min() < low or values.max() > high:
            off.append(name)
    note = ""
    if missing:
        note += "; no data: " + ", ".join(missing)
    if off:
        note += "; off the chart: " + ", ".join(off)
    return note
def fed_chart(period="1960–2026, all the data", countries=("United States",)):
    """Fig. 12.2: the policy rates of the chosen central banks over one period, U.S. recessions shaded."""
    x_range, y_range = PERIODS[period]
    part = rates[rates.country.isin(countries) & rates.date.between(x_range[0], x_range[1])]
    top = y_range[1]
    for step in [20, 40, 80]:                    # a wider axis only when a chosen country needs it
        if part.policy_rate.max() > top:
            top = step
    title = f"The fed funds rate: {peak.fedfunds:.1f}% at its 1981 peak, near zero in 2009–15 and 2020–21"
    if list(countries) != ["United States"]:
        title = "Central bank policy rates" + missing_or_off(part, "policy_rate", countries, y_range[0], top)
    fig = px.line(part, x="date", y="policy_rate", color="country", color_discrete_map=POLICY_COLORS, title=title,
                  labels={"date": "Year", "policy_rate": "Policy rate (percent)", "country": "Central bank of"})
    shade_recessions(fig, "1960-01-01")
    if "United States" in countries:
        fig.add_annotation(x=peak.date, y=peak.fedfunds, text=f"{peak.date:%B %Y}: {peak.fedfunds:.1f}%",
                           ax=90, ay=0, arrowhead=2)
        fig.add_annotation(x=latest.date, y=latest.fedfunds, text=f"{latest.date:%b %Y}: {latest.fedfunds:.2f}%",
                           ax=-40, ay=-50, arrowhead=2)
    fig.update_layout(xaxis_range=x_range, yaxis_range=[y_range[0], top], showlegend=len(countries) > 1)
    return fig

                                  description="countries", style=WIDE));

Sources. Data: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Federal Funds Effective Rate (FEDFUNDS), via FRED; Bank for International Settlements, Central bank policy rates (WS_CBPOL); recession bands: NBER-based Recession Indicators for the United States (USREC), via FRED, from the dates of the NBER Business Cycle Dating Committee. Prepared files: data/ch12/fig12-2.csv, data/ch12/policy_rates_monthly.csv, data/ch12/recessions.csv, data/ch12/countries.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 12.2 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

What to notice.

  • The rate has ranged from about 0.05 percent (2020–2021) to 19.1 percent (June 1981): the textbook’s “nearly 20 percent”.
  • Under Paul Volcker (Fed chair from 1979) the rate reached 17.6 percent in April 1980 and 18.9 percent in December 1980, and above 19 percent in 1981: the tight money that ended the Great Inflation (Figs. 10–12).
  • The rate was close to zero in 2009–2015 and again in 2020–2021, then rose quickly in 2022–2023 to fight the return of inflation. Rate cuts followed from September 2024.
  • The rate usually falls during and after recessions (the shaded bands): the Fed lowers it to stimulate the economy.
  • Add the euro area, the United Kingdom and Japan, and choose 2019–2026: the ECB’s rate was at zero and the Bank of Japan’s at −0.1 percent before the pandemic, and the Bank of England cut its rate to 0.1 percent in March 2020. The Bank of England raised its rate first (December 2021), then the Fed (March 2022) and the ECB (July 2022); the Bank of Japan waited until March 2024.

Fig. 3: The MP curve in the IS/MP diagram

Goal. Put the MP curve and the IS curve in one diagram and read off short-run output.

With sticky inflation, the central bank picks the real interest rate. The MP curve is simply a horizontal line at that rate. The IS curve then tells us the output that goes with it: the economy is where the two curves cross. This is the IS/MP diagram. When the central bank sets \(R = \bar{r}\) and there is no demand shock, the curves cross at \(\tilde{Y} = 0\), point \(A\): output is at potential.

The textbook uses this diagram for three figures: the starting point (Fig. 12.3), a higher interest rate (Fig. 12.4), and the Volcker tightening (Fig. 12.10). So we write one function, ismp_experiment, for all three. Its arguments are the new values: the real interest rate R_new that the central bank sets, the demand shock a_new and the slope b. With the defaults nothing changes. When a curve moves, the old one stays behind as a dashed gray line.

Python note. if ... else runs one block of lines or the other. (a_new, b) != (A_BAR, B_BAR) is true as soon as one of the two numbers differs from the baseline.

def ismp_experiment(R_new=R_BAR, a_new=A_BAR, b=B_BAR):
    """Figs. 12.3, 12.4, 12.10: the economy moves from A (R = r_bar, Y~ = 0) to B, where IS' meets MP'."""
    Y_B = is_curve(R_new, a_new, b)
    fig = go.Figure()
    if (a_new, b) != (A_BAR, B_BAR):
        add_is(fig, "IS", GRAY, dash="dash")
        add_is(fig, "IS′", TEAL, a_new, b)
    else:
        add_is(fig, "IS", TEAL)
    if R_new != R_BAR:
        add_line(fig, MP_X, [R_BAR, R_BAR], "MP", GRAY, "dash")
        add_line(fig, MP_X, [R_new, R_new], "MP′", BLUE)
        add_arrow(fig, -7.3, R_BAR, -7.3, R_new)                 # the central bank moves R
    else:
        add_line(fig, MP_X, [R_BAR, R_BAR], "MP", BLUE)
    add_point(fig, 0.0, R_BAR, "A", -8, 0)
    if (Y_B, R_new) != (0.0, R_BAR):
        add_point(fig, Y_B, R_new, "B", -8, 0)
        add_arrow(fig, 0.0, 0.6, Y_B, 0.6)                       # the change in output
    set_axes(fig, X_OUTPUT, Y_RATE)
    fig.update_layout(title=f"MP: R = {R_new:.2f}%;  IS: ā = {a_new:.1f}, b̄ = {b:.2f}  →  Ỹ = {Y_B:+.1f}%")
    return fig

Start with the textbook’s Fig. 12.3: the central bank sets \(R = \bar{r} = 5\) percent.

         a_new=FloatSlider(value=0.0, min=-2.0, max=2.0, step=0.5, description="demand shock ā", style=WIDE),
         b=FloatSlider(value=2.0, min=1.0, max=2.5, step=0.25, description="sensitivity of investment b̄", style=WIDE));
Show the code of the website version

slider_figure(ismp_experiment, "a_new", [-2.0, -1.0, 0.0, 1.0, 2.0], start=0.0, label="demand shock ā")

Source. Adapted from Fig. 12.3 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

What to notice.

  • At the baseline the MP line and the IS curve cross at \(A\): \(R = \bar{r} = 5\) percent and \(\tilde{Y} = 0\).
  • The central bank chooses the height of the MP line, nothing else. The IS curve then decides how much output that interest rate brings.
  • A demand shock moves the IS curve, and with \(R\) unchanged output moves one for one with \(\bar{a}\).

Fig. 4: Raising the interest rate in the IS/MP diagram

Goal. See how the central bank can cause a recession.

Inflation is slow to adjust, so a higher nominal interest rate means a higher real interest rate. The MP line moves up to \(R'\). Borrowing now costs more than the return on new capital (\(R' > \bar{r}\)), so firms and households cut their investment, and the economy moves along the IS curve from \(A\) to \(B\). The textbook’s figure has no numbers; with our baseline, \(R' = 6\) percent gives the “\(-2\) percent” of its later examples. It is the same function as in Fig. 3.

interact(ismp_experiment,
         R_new=FloatSlider(value=6.0, min=3.5, max=7.0, step=0.25, description="new real interest rate R′ (%)", style=WIDE),
         a_new=FloatSlider(value=0.0, min=-2.0, max=2.0, step=0.5, description="demand shock ā′", style=WIDE),
         b=FloatSlider(value=2.0, min=1.0, max=2.5, step=0.25, description="sensitivity of investment b̄", style=WIDE));
Show the code of the website version 
# @title Website version: Fig. 4 with a precomputed slider for the new real interest rate
slider_figure(ismp_experiment, "R_new", [5.0, 6.0, 6.5, 7.0], start=6.0, label="new real interest rate R′ (%)")

Source. Adapted from Fig. 12.4 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

What to notice.

  • With \(R' = 6\) percent, output falls from 0 to \(-2\) percent: each percentage point on \(R\) costs \(\bar{b} = 2\) points of output.
  • The IS curve does not move: a change in \(R\) is a movement along it. Only the MP line shifts.
  • A flatter IS curve (a larger \(\bar{b}\)) makes the same rate increase more painful: with \(\bar{b} = 2.5\) output falls to \(-2.5\) percent.

Your turn. The Fed wants to cool a booming economy with \(\bar{a} = 1.5\) and bring output exactly back to potential. How high must \(R'\) be? Set the sliders and check your answer with is_curve.

Hint

You need \(1.5 - 2\,(R' - 5) = 0\). Check with is_curve(5.75, a=1.5).

Fig. 5: Stabilizing the economy after a housing bubble

Goal. See how monetary policy can offset an aggregate demand shock.

When a housing bubble bursts, households lose wealth and confidence, and spend less: the demand shock \(\bar{a}\) falls to \(\bar{a}' < 0\). The IS curve shifts left, and at an unchanged interest rate the economy moves from \(A\) to \(B\), a recession (panel a; the textbook uses \(-2\) percent as its example). The central bank can respond by cutting the real interest rate to

\[R' = \bar{r} + \frac{\bar{a}'}{\bar{b}},\]

the rate at which the new IS curve gives \(\tilde{Y} = 0\) (our rate_for_output). Cheaper borrowing raises investment and makes up for the fall in \(\bar{a}\): the economy moves to \(C\), back at potential (panel b).

Python note. make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2, subplot_titles=(...)) makes a figure with two panels side by side. Our drawing functions take row and col, so add_point(..., 1, 2) draws in the panel of row 1, column 2. for col in [1, 2]: draws the parts that both panels share.

def housing_bubble(a_new=-2.0, b=B_BAR):
    """Fig. 12.5: (a) a fall in demand moves the economy from A to B; (b) the Fed lowers R to R' and reaches C."""
    Y_B = is_curve(R_BAR, a_new, b)
    R_new = rate_for_output(0.0, a_new, b)          # the rate at which IS' gives Y~ = 0
    fig = make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2, horizontal_spacing=0.12,
                        subplot_titles=("(a) The bubble bursts: A → B", "(b) The Fed lowers R: B → C"))
    for col in [1, 2]:
        add_is(fig, "IS", GRAY, A_BAR, b, "dash", 1, col)
        add_is(fig, "IS′", TEAL, a_new, b, "solid", 1, col)
        add_point(fig, 0.0, R_BAR, "A", -8, 0, 1, col)
        add_point(fig, Y_B, R_BAR, "B", -8, 0, 1, col)
        set_axes(fig, X_OUTPUT, Y_RATE, 1, col)
    add_line(fig, MP_X, [R_BAR, R_BAR], "MP", BLUE, "solid", 1, 1)
    add_arrow(fig, 0.0, 0.6, Y_B, 0.6, 1, 1)
    add_line(fig, MP_X, [R_BAR, R_BAR], "MP", GRAY, "dash", 1, 2)
    add_line(fig, MP_X, [R_new, R_new], "MP′", BLUE, "solid", 1, 2)
    add_arrow(fig, -7.3, R_BAR, -7.3, R_new, 1, 2)
    add_point(fig, 0.0, R_new, "C", -8, 0, 1, 2, where="bottom left")    # below left, clear of A
    add_arrow(fig, Y_B, 0.6, 0.0, 0.6, 1, 2)
    fig.update_layout(title=f"ā′ = {a_new:.1f}: B at Ỹ = {Y_B:+.1f}%;  R′ = {R_new:.2f}% brings C back to Ỹ = 0.0%")
    return fig
interact(housing_bubble,
         a_new=FloatSlider(value=-2.0, min=-3.0, max=-0.5, step=0.25, description="demand shock after the bust ā′", style=WIDE),
         b=FloatSlider(value=2.0, min=1.75, max=2.5, step=0.25, description="sensitivity of investment b̄", style=WIDE));
Show the code of the website version 
# @title Website version: Fig. 5 with a precomputed slider for the demand shock
slider_figure(housing_bubble, "a_new", [-3.0, -2.5, -2.0, -1.5, -1.0], start=-2.0, label="demand shock after the bust ā′")

Source. Adapted from Fig. 12.5 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

What to notice.

  • The bust alone (panel a) takes output to \(-2\) percent. Cutting \(R\) from 5 to 4 percent (panel b) brings it back to potential: in the model, monetary policy can fully offset a demand shock.
  • The larger the shock, the larger the cut. The flatter the IS curve (larger \(\bar{b}\)), the smaller the cut needed.
  • In practice this is hard. It takes time to see how large the shock is, and Milton Friedman’s “long and variable lags” mean that interest rates need 6–18 months to have their main effect. In 2008 the housing bust turned out to be much more than an ordinary demand shock (Chapter 14).

Your turn. Suppose the Fed waits and cuts \(R\) only to 4.5 percent. Where does output end up after a bust of \(\bar{a}' = -2\)? Compute it with is_curve.

Hint

The economy is on the new IS curve, so pass the new demand shock: is_curve(4.5, a=-2.0).

# Your turn: try it here

Fig. 6: The yield curve for U.S. Treasuries

Goal. See how interest rates at different maturities fit together, and what an inverted yield curve looks like.

The Fed sets an overnight rate, yet a firm that builds a factory borrows for years. The two are linked by the term structure of interest rates: a long-term interest rate is roughly the average of the short-term rates that investors expect over its life. Otherwise, buying one 5-year bond and buying five 1-year bonds in a row would pay different returns, and everyone would switch to the better one. The yield curve plots the interest rate (the yield) of government bonds against their maturity.

The first two days are the textbook’s curves; the third is the latest day in the data. To draw one line per day we need a long table, with one row per day and maturity.

Python note. melt turns columns into rows: each yield_... column becomes a value in the new column column, next to its yield. .map(MATURITY) replaces each column name by a readable label from the dictionary.

The file has no curves for 2024 and 2025, so the animation jumps from December 2023 to January 2026.

What to notice.

  • In January 2022 the Fed’s rate was near zero: short yields were close to 0 and rose steadily with maturity, the usual shape.
  • During 2022 the Fed raised its rate fast (Fig. 2). Short yields climbed above 4 percent, faster than long yields: by early 2023 the curve was inverted, with 5- and 10-year yields below the 1-month yield. Markets expected the Fed to lower rates over the next years.
  • By 2026 the curve slopes up again, at a higher level than in 2022.

Key numbers: the inversion

A common measure of the slope is the 10-year yield minus the 3-month yield. We compute it for every month.

Python note. pivot does the opposite of melt: it makes one row per date and one column per maturity (here the maturity in months), so wide[120] - wide[3] subtracts two columns.

wide = monthly.pivot(index="date", columns="months", values="yield")
spread = wide[120] - wide[3]                         # 10-year minus 3-month yield
print(f"First inverted month: {spread[spread < 0].index[0]};  most inverted: {spread.idxmin()} ({spread.min():.2f} points)")

The slope of the yield curve in other countries

Full yield curves are hard to find for many countries, but two points of the curve are not: the OECD publishes a 3-month interest rate (between banks) and the 10-year government bond yield for 47 economies since 2000. Their difference, the term spread, measures the slope of the yield curve: it is negative when the curve is inverted. For the United States it follows the Treasury curves above closely (the two 3-month rates differ by 0.18 points on average), and it also shows earlier inversions, in 2000, 2006–2007 and 2019, each followed by a recession.

yields = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "interest_rates_monthly.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
yields["spread"] = yields.rate_10y - yields.rate_3m        # 10-year minus 3-month rate

yields[yields.country == "United States"].tail(3)

Python note. .dropna(subset=["spread"]) drops the months in which one of the two rates is missing. The loop over [(-10, 15), (-20, 35)] widens both ends of the axis in two steps, only when a chosen country needs it.

def spread_chart(countries=("United States",)):
    """Fig. 12.6, extended: the term spread (10-year minus 3-month rate) of the chosen countries."""
    part = yields[yields.country.isin(countries)].dropna(subset=["spread"])
    low, high = -3, 5
    for wider_low, wider_high in [(-10, 15), (-20, 35)]:
        if part.spread.min() < low or part.spread.max() > high:
            low, high = wider_low, wider_high
    fig = px.line(part, x="date", y="spread", color="country", color_discrete_map=SPREAD_COLORS,
                  labels={"date": "Year", "spread": "10-year minus 3-month rate (points)", "country": "Country"},
                  title="Below zero, the yield curve is inverted" + missing_or_off(part, "spread", countries, low, high))
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_color="black", line_width=1)
    fig.update_layout(xaxis_range=["2000-01-01", "2026-12-31"], yaxis_range=[low, high], legend_title_text="")
    return fig

On the website, the buttons above the chart list a group of countries in the legend: click a country to add it.

Some lines jump far off the usual range: Greece (+28 points in February 2012, when investors feared a default on its 10-year bonds) or Russia (−18 points in January 2009, when short rates soared during a banking and currency crisis). A spread mixes expected future short rates with risk.

# Your turn: try it here

The Phillips curve

The Phillips curve links output to changes in inflation. We add a price shock, such as an oil price increase, and look at U.S. inflation over the long run.

Fig. 7: The Phillips curve

Goal. Draw the Phillips curve and see how the state of the economy changes inflation.

Imagine you run a firm and inflation has been 5 percent a year. You expect it to stay there, so normally you raise your prices by 5 percent. If demand for your products is weak, you raise them by less, to win back customers; if demand is strong, by more. When all firms do this, inflation equals last year’s inflation plus an adjustment for demand:

\[\Delta\pi_t = \bar{\nu}\,\tilde{Y}_t + \bar{o}.\]

A booming economy (\(\tilde{Y} > 0\)) raises inflation; a slumping one lowers it. The slope \(\bar{\nu}\) measures how strongly prices react to demand. As with the IS diagram, one function draws three textbook figures: the Phillips curve itself (12.7), an oil shock (12.8) and a recession (12.11). Its arguments are short-run output Y_new, the price shock o_new and the slope nu.

Python note. for x, y, anchor, text in REGIONS: takes the list of (x, y, anchor, text) groups one at a time and unpacks each into four names. dict(X_OUTPUT, title=...) copies the settings of X_OUTPUT and replaces the title. Y_DPI if fits else Y_DPI_WIDE is a one-line if: it gives the first axis when fits is true (both conditions joined by and hold) and the wider one otherwise. yaxis["range"][1] looks up the axis range and takes its second number, the top of the axis.

REGIONS = [(-7.6, 3.4, "left", "Δπ > 0:<br>inflation rises"), (7.6, -3.4, "right", "Δπ < 0:<br>inflation falls")]
X_SLUMP_BOOM = dict(X_OUTPUT, title="←  Below potential (slump)          Short-run output, Ỹ (%)          Above potential (boom)  →")


def pc_experiment(Y_new=0.0, o_new=O_BAR, nu=NU):
    """Figs. 12.7, 12.8, 12.11: the Phillips curve, a price shock o' that shifts it, and the economy at Y~."""
    dpi = phillips(Y_new, nu, o_new)
    fits = abs(dpi) <= 3.4 and abs(phillips(2.0, nu, o_new)) <= 3.4
    yaxis = Y_DPI if fits else Y_DPI_WIDE                  # a wider axis only when B or the shift would not fit
    top = yaxis["range"][1]
    fig = go.Figure()
    if o_new != O_BAR:
        add_pc(fig, "PC", GRAY, nu, O_BAR, "dash", top=top)
        add_pc(fig, "PC′", GREEN, nu, o_new, top=top)
        add_arrow(fig, 2.0, phillips(2.0, nu), 2.0, phillips(2.0, nu, o_new))      # the shift of the curve
    else:
        add_pc(fig, "Phillips curve", GREEN, nu, top=top)
    add_point(fig, 0.0, phillips(0.0, nu, o_new), "A", -8, -top, where="top left")  # top left: off the rising curve
    if Y_new != 0.0:
        add_point(fig, Y_new, dpi, "B", -8, -top, where="top left")
        add_arrow(fig, 0.0, 0.3 - top, Y_new, 0.3 - top)                            # the change in output
    for x, y, anchor, text in REGIONS:
        fig.add_annotation(x=x, y=y, text=text, showarrow=False, xanchor=anchor, font=dict(size=13, color=GRAY))
    set_axes(fig, X_SLUMP_BOOM, yaxis)
    fig.update_layout(title=f"Ỹ = {Y_new:+.1f}%, ō = {o_new:+.1f}  →  Δπ = {nu:.2f} × ({Y_new:+.1f}) + ({o_new:+.1f}) = {dpi:+.2f}")
    return fig
interact(pc_experiment,
         Y_new=FloatSlider(value=2.0, min=-4.0, max=4.0, step=0.5, description="short-run output Ỹ (%)", style=WIDE),
         o_new=FloatSlider(value=0.0, min=-2.0, max=2.0, step=0.5, description="price shock ō", style=WIDE),
         nu=FloatSlider(value=0.5, min=0.25, max=1.0, step=0.05, description="slope ν̄", style=WIDE));
Show the code of the website version 
# @title Website version: Fig. 7 with a precomputed slider for short-run output
slider_figure(pc_experiment, "Y_new", [-4.0, -3.0, -2.0, -1.0, 0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0], start=2.0,
              label="short-run output Ỹ (%)")

Source. Adapted from Fig. 12.7 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

What to notice.

  • At potential (\(\tilde{Y} = 0\), point \(A\)) inflation is steady: this year’s inflation equals last year’s.
  • An economy 2 percent above potential raises inflation by \(0.5 \times 2 = 1\) point a year, and it keeps rising as long as the boom lasts.
  • A steeper curve (larger \(\bar{\nu}\)) means prices react more to demand. With a flat curve it takes a deep recession to lower inflation by one point.

A brief history. A. W. Phillips first related the level of (wage) inflation to economic activity. In the 1960s many economists concluded that a country could keep output high for ever by accepting, say, 5 instead of 2 percent inflation. Milton Friedman and Edmund Phelps argued that firms would soon build the higher inflation into their prices: holding output above potential would make inflation rise year after year, which is the version of the curve used here. The rising inflation of the 1970s proved them right.

Your turn. With the baseline slope, how far below potential must output be to lower inflation by 1.5 points in one year? Find it with the sliders, then check it with phillips.

Hint

Solve \(-1.5 = 0.5\,\tilde{Y}\). Then try phillips(-3.0).

# Your turn: try it here

Fig. 8: An oil price increase

Goal. See how a price shock moves inflation even when output is at potential.

When oil prices jump, gasoline, airline tickets and heating cost more at once, and firms that use oil as an input pass the higher cost on to their prices. In the model this is a positive price shock \(\bar{o}\): the Phillips curve shifts up by \(\bar{o}\) for one period. Even at potential, inflation now rises by \(\bar{o}\). Economists call such increases cost-push inflation, and the \(\bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}\) term demand-pull inflation. Price shocks can also come from other inputs (steel), from large union wage settlements (\(\bar{o} > 0\)), or from a large inflow of workers that holds wages down (\(\bar{o} < 0\)). The textbook’s figure has no number; we use \(\bar{o} = 1\) point.

interact(pc_experiment,
         Y_new=FloatSlider(value=0.0, min=-4.0, max=4.0, step=0.5, description="short-run output Ỹ (%)", style=WIDE),
         o_new=FloatSlider(value=1.0, min=-2.0, max=2.0, step=0.5, description="price shock ō", style=WIDE),
         nu=FloatSlider(value=0.5, min=0.25, max=1.0, step=0.05, description="slope ν̄", style=WIDE));
Show the code of the website version 
# @title Website version: Fig. 8 with a precomputed slider for the price shock
slider_figure(pc_experiment, "o_new", [-2.0, -1.0, 0.0, 1.0, 2.0], start=1.0, label="price shock ō")

Source. Adapted from Fig. 12.8 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

What to notice.

  • The whole curve moves up by \(\bar{o}\): at \(\tilde{Y} = 0\), inflation rises by 1 point.
  • To keep inflation steady after the shock, output would have to fall to \(\tilde{Y} = -\bar{o}/\bar{\nu} = -2\) percent: a price shock confronts the central bank with a hard choice.
  • Quantity theory or Phillips curve? Chapter 8 found that faster growth of real GDP lowers inflation; here a boom raises it. The two are about different things: the quantity theory is a long-run model in which more output means more supply of goods; here higher short-run output means more demand than the economy’s potential.

Key numbers: demand-pull and cost-push

The change in inflation has two parts, \(\bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}\) and \(\bar{o}\). A loop computes them for a few cases.

for Y, o in [(0.0, 1.0), (2.0, 0.0), (2.0, 1.0), (-2.0, 1.0)]:
    print(f"Y~ = {Y:+.1f}%, o = {o:+.1f}:  demand-pull {phillips(Y, o=0.0):+.2f} + cost-push {o:+.2f}"
          f" = {phillips(Y, o=o):+.2f} points")
Y~ = +0.0%, o = +1.0:  demand-pull +0.00 + cost-push +1.00 = +1.00 points
Y~ = +2.0%, o = +0.0:  demand-pull +1.00 + cost-push +0.00 = +1.00 points
Y~ = +2.0%, o = +1.0:  demand-pull +1.00 + cost-push +1.00 = +2.00 points
Y~ = -2.0%, o = +1.0:  demand-pull -1.00 + cost-push +1.00 = +0.00 points

The last line is the hard case: a recession of 2 percent exactly offsets an oil shock of 1 point.

First phillips(0.0, o=-0.5). For steady inflation solve \(0 = 0.5\,\tilde{Y} - 0.5\).

Fig. 9: Inflation in the United States

Goal. Look at U.S. inflation since 1960 and at the role of monetary policy in it.

inflation = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig12-9.csv")
inflation.tail()
year inflation_cpi
61 2021 4.68124

inflation_cpi is the percent change in the average consumer price index of each year. One data note: the October 2025 CPI was never collected (the federal government was shut down), so the 2025 value averages the other 11 months.

We add the fed funds rate of Fig. 2, averaged over each year, and the real interest rate from the Fisher equation, \(R = i - \pi\). This is the ex post real rate, computed with the inflation that actually happened. Investors decide with the inflation they expect (the ex ante rate), but in this chapter we ignore the difference.

Python note. groupby(...) puts the months of each year in one group, and .mean() averages each group. .map(annual_ff) then looks up the average for each year of the inflation table. pd.to_datetime turns the year into a date (1 January), so the chart can shade the recessions.

annual_ff = fedfunds.groupby(fedfunds.date.dt.year).fedfunds.mean()
inflation["fed_funds"] = inflation.year.map(annual_ff)
inflation["real_rate"] = real_rate(inflation.fed_funds, inflation.inflation_cpi)
inflation["date"] = pd.to_datetime(inflation.year.astype(str))
top = inflation.loc[inflation.inflation_cpi.idxmax()]
inflation[inflation.year.between(1978, 1984)].round(2)

The file inflation_annual.csv has the CPI inflation rate of 194 economies from the World Bank (for the United States, the numbers above), and the policy rates of Fig. 2 give the interest rate for 49 of them. We average the monthly policy rates over each year and join the two tables.

Python note. rates.assign(year=...) returns a copy of rates with a new column year. merge joins two tables on the columns they share, here country and year; how="left" keeps every row of the left table, prices, and leaves the policy rate empty (NaN) where a country has none.

world = prices.merge(annual_rates, on=["country", "year"], how="left")
world["real_rate"] = real_rate(world.policy_rate, world.inflation)
world["date"] = pd.to_datetime(world.year.astype(str))

The U.S. rows repeat the table above. The chart shows inflation as a filled area. Click the legend to add the policy rate and the real interest rate, and choose another country from the menu.

def inflation_chart(country="United States"):
    """Fig. 12.9: inflation, the policy rate i and the real interest rate R = i − π of one country."""
    part = world[world.country == country]
    worst = part.loc[part.inflation.idxmax()]
    low, high = -8, 18
    for wider_low, wider_high in [(-20, 40), (-50, 100)]:   # a wider axis only when the country needs it
        if part.inflation.max() > high or part.policy_rate.max() > high or part.real_rate.min() < low:
            low, high = wider_low, wider_high
    title = f"{country}: inflation peaked at {worst.inflation:.1f}% in {worst.year}"
    if country == "United States":
        title = f"Inflation peaked at {worst.inflation:.1f}% in {worst.year} and tends to fall after shaded recessions"
    if part.inflation.max() > high or part.policy_rate.max() > high or part.real_rate.min() < low:
        title += " (off the chart)"
    fig = px.area(part, x="date", y="inflation", labels={"date": "Year", "inflation": "Percent"}, title=title)
    fig.update_traces(name="Inflation (CPI)", showlegend=True, line_color=TEAL)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=part.date, y=part.policy_rate, visible="legendonly", line=dict(color=BLUE, width=2),
                             name="Fed funds rate, i" if country == "United States" else "Policy rate, i"))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=part.date, y=part.real_rate, name="Real interest rate, R = i − π",
                             visible="legendonly", line=dict(color=GREEN, width=2, dash="dot")))
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color="black", line_width=1)
    if country == "United States":
        shade_recessions(fig, "1960-01-01")
    fig.update_layout(xaxis_range=["1959-01-01", "2026-12-31"], yaxis_range=[low, high],
                      legend=dict(x=0.99, y=0.98, xanchor="right", yanchor="top"))
    return fig

Data: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers: All Items (CPIAUCSL), via FRED; World Bank, World Development Indicators, Inflation, consumer prices (annual %) (FP.CPI.TOTL.ZG); Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Federal Funds Effective Rate (FEDFUNDS), via FRED; Bank for International Settlements, Central bank policy rates (WS_CBPOL); recession bands: NBER-based Recession Indicators for the United States (USREC), via FRED, from the dates of the NBER Business Cycle Dating Committee. Prepared files: data/ch12/fig12-9.csv, data/ch12/inflation_annual.csv, data/ch12/fig12-2.csv, data/ch12/policy_rates_monthly.csv, data/ch12/recessions.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 12.9 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

What to notice.

  • Inflation was low in the early 1960s (1.1 to 1.5 percent; the textbook’s “about 2 percent” is generous), rose to 11.0 percent in 1974 and peaked at 13.5 percent in 1980, then fell to 3.2 percent by 1983: the Volcker disinflation.
  • Turn on the real interest rate: it was close to zero in 1979–1980 and jumped to about 6 percent in 1981–1984. That is the tight monetary policy of Figs. 10–12.
  • Inflation usually falls after recessions (the shaded bands), as the Phillips curve predicts.
  • In 2021–2022 inflation returned (8.0 percent in 2022), while the real interest rate was deeply negative: monetary policy was very loose (Fig. 15).
  • Choose Türkiye: in 2022 inflation reached 72 percent while the policy rate averaged 12.6 percent, a real interest rate of about −60 percent. Only after the central bank raised its rate to about 49 percent in 2024 did inflation start to fall (35 percent in 2025).

# Your turn: try it here

Using the short-run model: disinflation and the Great Inflation

Now we put the three pieces together and run the model through time, first for the Volcker disinflation of the early 1980s and then for a policy mistake of the 1970s.

Fig. 10: Tightening monetary policy

Goal. Follow the first step of the Volcker disinflation in the IS/MP diagram.

By 1979 inflation exceeded 10 percent. Paul Volcker’s Fed slowed money growth, which means raising the nominal interest rate. Because inflation is sticky, the real rate rises too: \(R' = i' - \pi\). With inflation at 10 percent, a nominal rate of 15 percent keeps \(R = 5\% = \bar{r}\); raising it to 16 percent lifts the real rate to 6 percent, and output falls to the textbook’s \(-2\) percent. The function reuses ismp_experiment and only adds the Fisher step.

def tightening(i_new=16.0, pi=10.0):
    """Fig. 12.10: with sticky inflation pi, a higher nominal rate i' raises R' = i' - pi and lowers output."""
    R_new = real_rate(i_new, pi)
    fig = ismp_experiment(R_new=R_new)
    fig.update_layout(title=f"i′ = {i_new:.1f}% and sticky π = {pi:.1f}%  →  R′ = {R_new:.1f}%  →  Ỹ = {is_curve(R_new):+.1f}%")
    return fig
interact(tightening,
         i_new=FloatSlider(value=16.0, min=13.0, max=17.5, step=0.5, description="new nominal interest rate i′ (%)", style=WIDE),
         pi=FloatSlider(value=10.0, min=9.0, max=11.0, step=0.5, description="sticky inflation π (%)", style=WIDE));
Show the code of the website version 
# @title Website version: Fig. 10 with a precomputed slider for the nominal interest rate
slider_figure(tightening, "i_new", [15.0, 15.5, 16.0, 16.5, 17.0, 17.5], start=16.0, label="new nominal interest rate i′ (%)")

Source. Adapted from Fig. 12.10 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

What to notice.

  • Only the real rate matters for output: \(i' = 16\) with \(\pi = 10\) has the same effect as \(i' = 7\) with \(\pi = 1\).
  • If inflation were not sticky (if the classical dichotomy held even in the short run), a higher nominal rate could simply come with lower inflation and leave output alone. Stickiness is what gives monetary policy real effects.
  • In 1981 the effective fed funds rate averaged 16.4 percent, and the real rate was about 6 percent (Fig. 9): the deepest recession in decades followed.

Fig. 11: A recession and falling inflation

Goal. Follow the second step: the recession lowers inflation through the Phillips curve.

The Fed’s recession takes output to \(\tilde{Y}' = -2\) percent. Firms see demand fall, so they raise prices less aggressively, and the economy jumps from \(A\) to \(B\) on the Phillips curve, where \(\Delta\pi' < 0\). It is the pc_experiment function again, now with output below potential.

Source. Adapted from Fig. 12.11 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

What to notice.

  • With \(\bar{\nu} = 0.5\), a recession of 2 percent lowers inflation by 1 point: from 10 to 9 percent in the first year.
  • The textbook’s example, “instead of raising prices by 10 percent, they may raise them by only 8 percent”, is a fall of 2 points; it corresponds to \(\bar{\nu} = 1\). Move the slope slider to 1 to see it.
  • The cost of lower inflation is lost output; the steeper the curve, the cheaper the disinflation.

# Your turn: try it here

Fig. 12: The disinflation over time

Goal. Run the Volcker policy year by year and watch inflation come down.

The Fed raises the real interest rate in year 0 and keeps it high until year \(t^*\), when inflation has fallen enough; then it returns \(R\) to \(\bar{r}\). Each year the model takes three steps: the MP curve sets \(R_t\), the IS curve gives \(\tilde{Y}_t\), and the Phillips curve gives \(\pi_t = \pi_{t-1} + \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t\). That is exactly our simulate function. Inflation starts at the textbook’s 10 percent. Inflation in year 0 already falls, because \(\pi_0 = (P_1 - P_0)/P_0\): firms set next year’s prices when they see this year’s recession.

Python note. np.arange(-2, 10) is the years \(-2, -1, \ldots, 9\). np.where(condition, a, b) gives a where the condition is true and b elsewhere: here a high rate from year 0 to \(t^* - 1\) and \(\bar{r}\) otherwise. & means “and”. line_shape="hv" draws steps: a flat line, then a jump. IntSlider is a slider for whole numbers. pi_path.min() is the smallest number in the array: if a long, deep recession pushes inflation below zero (deflation), the inflation axis extends below zero to show it.

def disinflation(Y_rec=-2.0, t_star=5, nu=NU):
    """Fig. 12.12: the Fed holds R high from year 0 to t*; output is Y_rec and inflation falls from 10%."""
    years = np.arange(-2, 10)
    R_path = np.where((years >= 0) & (years < t_star), rate_for_output(Y_rec), R_BAR)
    Y_path, pi_path = simulate(R_path, pi_start=10.0, nu=nu)
    fig = make_subplots(rows=1, cols=3, horizontal_spacing=0.09,
                        subplot_titles=("(a) R held high until t*", "(b) Output below potential", "(c) Inflation steps down"))
    paths = [R_path, Y_path, pi_path]
    colors, shapes = [BLUE, TEAL, GREEN], ["hv", "hv", "linear"]
    axes = [dict(title="Real interest rate, R (%)", range=[2.5, 7.5]), dict(title="Short-run output, Ỹ (%)", range=[-4.5, 1.5]),
            dict(title="Inflation, π (%)", range=[min(0.0, pi_path.min() - 1.0), 11.5])]   # widens only below zero
    for k in range(3):
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=years, y=paths[k], mode="lines+markers", showlegend=False, line_shape=shapes[k],
                                 line=dict(color=colors[k], width=4), marker=dict(color="black", size=9)), row=1, col=k + 1)
        set_axes(fig, dict(title="Year", tickvals=[0, t_star], ticktext=["0", "t*"], range=[-2.5, 9.5]), axes[k], 1, k + 1)
    fig.update_layout(title=f"π: 10.0% → {pi_path[-1]:.1f}% with Ỹ = {Y_rec:+.1f}% until t* = {t_star};"
                            f"  output lost: {-Y_path.sum():.1f} %-years")
    return fig

Source. Adapted from Fig. 12.12 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

What to notice.

  • Five years at \(\tilde{Y} = -2\) percent bring inflation from 10 to 5 percent, one point a year. When the Fed returns \(R\) to \(\bar{r}\), output goes back to potential and inflation stays at its new, lower level.
  • The price is 10 “percent-years” of lost output: 2 percent of GDP for five years, or 2 percent-years for each point of inflation removed.
  • A deeper recession gets there faster, at about the same total cost: with \(\tilde{Y} = -4\) it takes 2.5 years. Only a steeper Phillips curve makes the disinflation cheaper.
  • In reality, inflation fell from 13.5 percent in 1980 to 3.2 percent in 1983 (Fig. 9), faster than in this example, and the recession of 1981–1982 was the deepest in decades.

Fig. 13: Mistaking a slowdown in potential for a recession

Goal. See how a slowdown in potential output, mistaken for a recession, can feed inflation.

From the early 1970s, U.S. productivity growth slowed down, so potential output grew more slowly. At the time, policymakers thought potential output was still growing at its old rate. They saw actual output fall behind that believed path, read it as a recession (\(\tilde{Y}_{\text{perceived}} < 0\)), and lowered interest rates. In truth output was then above its true potential (\(\tilde{Y}_{\text{true}} > 0\)), and through the Phillips curve inflation rose.

The textbook’s figure is stylized, so we describe it with three numbers: potential growth before 1973 (g_old), after 1973 (g_new), and how far the stimulus eventually pushes output above true potential (gap_max, reached gradually). Output is an index with 1973 = 100. This small model is used only here, so we define it in this section.

Python note. np.exp is the exponential function: an index growing at g percent a year is \(100\,e^{g\,(t - 1973)/100}\). np.minimum(x, 0) keeps the negative values of x and sets the others to 0, and np.maximum(x, 0) does the opposite. continue skips the rest of the loop for the current item.

def output_paths(g_old=3.5, g_new=2.5, gap_max=4.0):
    """Fig. 12.13: believed potential, true potential and actual output (1973 = 100)."""
    years = np.arange(1965, 1986)
    before, after = np.minimum(years - 1973, 0), np.maximum(years - 1973, 0)
    believed = 100 * np.exp(g_old * (years - 1973) / 100)
    true = 100 * np.exp((g_old * before + g_new * after) / 100)
    gap_true = gap_max * (1 - np.exp(-after / 4))      # the stimulus pushes output above true potential
    actual = true * (1 + gap_true / 100)
    return years, believed, true, actual
def slowdown(g_old=3.5, g_new=2.5, gap_max=4.0):
    """Fig. 12.13 with readouts: the perceived and the true output gap, and the rise in inflation."""
    years, believed, true, actual = output_paths(g_old, g_new, gap_max)
    perceived_gap, true_gap = 100 * (actual / believed - 1), 100 * (actual / true - 1)
    dpi = phillips(true_gap[(years > 1973) & (years <= 1980)]).sum()   # Phillips curve, 1974-1980
    fig = go.Figure()
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=years, y=believed, name=f"Believed potential ({g_old:g}% a year)", line=dict(color=GREEN, width=4, dash="dash")))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=years, y=actual, name="Actual output (with the stimulus)", line=dict(color=TEAL, width=4)))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=years, y=true, name=f"True potential ({g_new:g}% a year after 1973)", line=dict(color=BLUE, width=4, dash="dash")))
    gaps = [(actual[-1], believed[-1], "seen as Ỹ < 0"), (true[-1], actual[-1], "true Ỹ > 0")]
    for low, high, text in gaps:
        if high - low < 4:                             # no bracket (and no false label) for a gap that is not there
            continue
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[1985.4, 1985.4], y=[low, high], mode="lines", showlegend=False, line=dict(color="black", width=2)))
        fig.add_annotation(x=1985.6, y=(low + high) / 2, text=text, showarrow=False, xanchor="left", font=dict(size=13))
    k = 1980 - 1965                                    # the position of 1980 in the arrays
    fig.add_vline(x=1973, line_dash="dot", line_color=GRAY)
    fig.update_layout(title=f"1980: perceived Ỹ = {perceived_gap[k]:+.1f}%, true Ỹ = {true_gap[k]:+.1f}%;"
                            f" inflation +{dpi:.1f} points since 1973",
                      xaxis=dict(title="Year", range=[1964, 1990], tickvals=[1965, 1970, 1973, 1980, 1985]),
                      yaxis=dict(title="Output (index, 1973 = 100)", range=[60, 190]),
                      legend=dict(x=0.01, y=0.99, xanchor="left", yanchor="top"))
    return fig
interact(slowdown,
         g_old=FloatSlider(value=3.5, min=2.0, max=5.0, step=0.25, description="potential growth before 1973 (%)", style=WIDE),
         g_new=FloatSlider(value=2.5, min=1.0, max=4.0, step=0.25, description="true potential growth after 1973 (%)", style=WIDE),
         gap_max=FloatSlider(value=4.0, min=0.0, max=6.0, step=0.5, description="stimulus: long-run true gap (%)", style=WIDE));

slider_figure(slowdown, "g_new", [1.5, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0, 3.5], start=2.5, label="true potential growth after 1973 (%)")

Source. Adapted from Fig. 12.13 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

What to notice.

  • By 1980 actual output is 3.7 percent below the believed path, so policymakers see a recession and keep stimulating. Yet it is 3.3 percent above true potential.
  • The true gap is positive every year after 1973, so the Phillips curve raises inflation every year: about 8 points by 1980 with \(\bar{\nu} = 0.5\). Actual U.S. inflation rose from 6.3 percent in 1973 to 13.5 percent in 1980, also helped by the oil shocks of 1974 and 1979.
  • Set the growth rate after 1973 equal to the one before: there is no slowdown, the two dashed paths coincide, and the stimulus is plainly a boom.
  • Policymakers learn of their mistake through rising inflation, but oil shocks also raise inflation, which made the lesson slow to learn.

The short-run model in a nutshell

The textbook sums up how monetary policy works through the three building blocks:

Building block Step
MP curve \(\uparrow i_t \Rightarrow \uparrow R_t\)
IS curve \(\uparrow R_t \Rightarrow \downarrow \tilde{Y}_t\)
Phillips curve \(\downarrow \tilde{Y}_t \Rightarrow \downarrow \Delta\pi_t\)

Here is the chain in numbers, with inflation stuck at 10 percent, for three nominal interest rates.

rows = []
for i in [15.0, 16.0, 17.0]:
    R = real_rate(i, 10.0)
    Y = is_curve(R)
    rows.append([i, R, Y, phillips(Y)])
pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["nominal rate i (%)", "real rate R (%)", "output Y~ (%)", "change in inflation (points)"])
nominal rate i (%) real rate R (%) output Y~ (%) change in inflation (points)
0 15.0 5.0 0.0 0.0
1 16.0 6.0 -2.0 -1.0
2 17.0 7.0 -4.0 -2.0

The Covid-19 recession

The pandemic tested the model: a deep but brief fall in GDP, a large fiscal response, and the return of inflation. These figures show it in the data.

Fig. 14: Real GDP in the United States

Goal. Measure how deep the Covid-19 recession was and how fast GDP came back.

gdp = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig12-14.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
gdp.head()
date real_gdp
0 2015-01-01 18.6666
1 2015-04-01 18.7822

Each row is a quarter. real_gdp is real GDP in trillions of chained 2017 dollars, at an annual rate. The textbook used 2012 dollars, so its numbers are 8–10 percent lower; the shape is the same. To judge whether GDP was “back on trend”, we fit a straight line to the logarithm of GDP before Covid (2015Q1–2019Q4), which means a constant growth rate, and extend it.

Python note. np.polyfit(x, y, 1) fits a straight line \(y = \text{slope}\cdot x + \text{intercept}\) by least squares. np.log and np.exp move between levels and logs; np.exp(4 * slope) turns quarterly log growth into annual growth.

pre = gdp[gdp.date <= "2019-10-01"]                     # 2015Q1 to 2019Q4
t = np.arange(len(gdp))                                 # quarters since 2015Q1
slope, intercept = np.polyfit(t[:len(pre)], np.log(pre.real_gdp), 1)
gdp["trend"] = np.exp(intercept + slope * t)
gdp["gap"] = 100 * (gdp.real_gdp / gdp.trend - 1)       # percent above (+) or below (-) the trend
fall = 100 * (gdp.real_gdp[gdp.date == "2020-04-01"].iloc[0] / gdp.real_gdp[gdp.date == "2019-10-01"].iloc[0] - 1)
print(f"Pre-Covid trend growth: {100 * (np.exp(4 * slope) - 1):.2f}% a year;  2019Q4 to 2020Q2: {fall:.2f}%")
gdp[gdp.date.dt.year.between(2020, 2022)].round(2)
