fig.update_traces(line_dash="dash", marker_size=4, selector=dict(name="Pre-Covid trend (2015–2019)"))
shade_recessions(fig, "2015-01-01")
fig.update_layout(yaxis_range=[18, 25.5], legend=dict(x=0.01, y=0.99, xanchor="left", yanchor="top", title=None))
fig.show()

Sources. Data: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, Real Gross Domestic Product (GDPC1), via FRED; recession bands: NBER-based Recession Indicators for the United States (USREC), via FRED, from the dates of the NBER Business Cycle Dating Committee. Prepared files: data/ch12/fig12-14.csv, data/ch12/recessions.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 12.14 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

What to notice.

  • From 2019Q4 to 2020Q2 real GDP fell by 9.1 percent, the textbook’s “more than 10 percent” in round numbers (9.6 percent in the data of 2023).
  • The rebound was just as remarkable: from 2021Q2 on, GDP has stayed within about 1 percent of its pre-Covid trend. It was 0.3 percent above the trend in 2021Q4, but it never rose sharply above it.
  • Before Covid, real GDP grew by about 2.5 percent a year.

Real GDP in other countries

GDP levels in different currencies cannot be compared directly, but their changes can. The OECD publishes a quarterly volume index of real GDP for 49 economies (China is missing: it does not publish seasonally adjusted levels). We set every country’s index to 100 in 2019Q4, just before the pandemic, so each line shows the percent change since then.

Python note. base is a Series with one value per country, the index in 2019Q4. gdp_world.country.map(base) looks up that value for every row, so dividing by it rebases each country’s index to 100 in 2019Q4.

gdp_world = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "gdp_quarterly.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
base = gdp_world[gdp_world.date == "2019-10-01"].set_index("country").gdp_index
gdp_world["index_2019q4"] = 100 * gdp_world.gdp_index / gdp_world.country.map(base)
GDP_COLORS = menu_colors(sorted(gdp_world.country.unique()))
gdp_world[(gdp_world.country == "United States") & (gdp_world.date.dt.year == 2020)].round(2)
iso3 country date gdp_index index_2019q4
2209 USA United States 2020-01-01 102.09 98.68
2210 USA United States 2020-04-01 94.05 90.91
2211 USA United States 2020-07-01 101.35 97.97
2212 USA United States 2020-10-01 102.50 99.08

The U.S. index falls by the same 9.1 percent as the textbook series from 2019Q4 to 2020Q2: it is the same GDP data.

def gdp_index_chart(countries=("United States",)):
    """Fig. 12.14, extended: real GDP of the chosen countries, 2019Q4 = 100."""
    part = gdp_world[gdp_world.country.isin(countries)]
    low, high = 80, 120
    for wider_low, wider_high in [(70, 130), (60, 160)]:   # a wider axis only when a chosen country needs it
        if part.index_2019q4.min() < low or part.index_2019q4.max() > high:
            low, high = wider_low, wider_high
    title = "Real GDP since the end of 2019 (2019Q4 = 100)"
    if len(countries) == 1 and len(part) > 0:
        fall = 100 - part.index_2019q4[part.date.dt.year == 2020].min()
        title = f"{countries[0]}: real GDP fell {fall:.1f}% in 2020 (2019Q4 = 100)"
    title += missing_or_off(part, "index_2019q4", countries, low, high)
    fig = px.line(part, x="date", y="index_2019q4", color="country", color_discrete_map=GDP_COLORS, markers=True,
                  labels={"date": "Year", "index_2019q4": "Real GDP, 2019Q4 = 100", "country": "Country"}, title=title)
    fig.update_traces(marker_size=4)
    fig.add_hline(y=100, line_dash="dot", line_color=GRAY)
    fig.update_layout(xaxis_range=["2014-10-01", "2026-10-01"], yaxis_range=[low, high], legend_title_text="")
    return fig

On the website, the buttons above the chart list a group of countries in the legend: click a country to add it.

Sources. Data: OECD, Quarterly National Accounts (DSD_NAMAIN1@DF_QNA), real GDP, chain-linked volume index, on the OECD Data Explorer. Prepared files: data/ch12/gdp_quarterly.csv, data/ch12/countries.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 12.14 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

  • Add the United Kingdom and Spain: their real GDP fell by about 22 percent in 2020, more than twice as much as in the United States, and Spain was back at its 2019Q4 level only in 2022Q2. Longer lockdowns, and in Spain a large tourism sector, made the fall deeper.

Each row is a month. inflation_all is the percent change of the consumer price index over the previous 12 months, and inflation_core the same for core prices, which leave out food and energy, the most volatile prices. Are any values missing?

Python note. .isna() is true where a value is missing, and .any(axis=1) is true for rows with at least one missing value.

October 2025 is empty: the federal government was shut down that month and the Bureau of Labor Statistics did not collect prices. We keep the gap rather than invent a number; the chart simply breaks the lines there.

The pandemic inflation was not only American. The file cpi_monthly.csv has the same two rates for 64 economies: all items from the Bank for International Settlements (national consumer price indexes; for the euro area, the harmonised index the ECB targets), and core inflation from the OECD (from Eurostat for the euro area). Core data are missing for some countries and stop early for others: in 2026 the OECD has not yet published core inflation for the European countries, and its core index for Japan stops in June 2021. The U.S. rows are the table above.

cpi_world = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "cpi_monthly.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
cpi_world.groupby("country").inflation_core.count().sort_values().head(8)     # months with core data

Name: inflation_core, dtype: int64

Python note. .set_index("date")["All items"] makes a Series labelled by date, so .idxmin() and .idxmax() return dates. f"{day:%B %Y}" writes a date as month and year. The loop over the list of ranges keeps the first one that holds every value of the chosen country.

def cpi_chart(country="United States"):
    """Fig. 12.15: 12-month CPI inflation, all items and core, of one country since January 2020."""
    part = cpi_world[cpi_world.country == country].rename(
        columns={"inflation_all": "All items", "inflation_core": "Core (less food and energy)"})
    values = part[["All items", "Core (less food and energy)"]]
    for low, high in [(0, 10), (-4, 12), (-5, 30), (-10, 100), (-20, 300)]:
        if values.min().min() >= low and values.max().max() <= high:
            break                                       # the first range that holds every value
    title = "No all-items CPI data for this country"
    every = part.set_index("date")["All items"].dropna()
    if not every.empty:
        dip = every[every.index.year == 2020]
        later = every[every.index > dip.idxmin()]
        title = f"CPI inflation fell to {round(dip.min(), 1) + 0.0:.1f}% in {dip.idxmin():%B %Y}"
        if not later.empty:
            title += f", then rose to {later.max():.1f}% in {later.idxmax():%B %Y}"
    fig = px.line(part, x="date", y=["All items", "Core (less food and energy)"], title=title,
                  labels={"date": "Year", "value": "Percent change over 12 months", "variable": "CPI"})
    fig.update_traces(line_width=3)
    fig.add_hline(y=2, line_dash="dot", line_color=GRAY, annotation_text="2 percent", annotation_position="bottom right")
    if country == "United States":
        shade_recessions(fig, "2020-01-01")
    fig.update_layout(xaxis_range=["2019-12-01", "2026-10-31"], yaxis_range=[low, high], legend_title_text=country,
                      legend=dict(x=0.99, y=0.98, xanchor="right", yanchor="top"))
    return fig
interact(cpi_chart, country=Dropdown(options=sorted(cpi_world.country.unique()), value="United States",
                                     description="country", style=WIDE));

Sources. Data: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers: All Items (CPIAUCSL), via FRED; U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, CPI for All Urban Consumers: All Items Less Food and Energy (CPILFESL), via FRED; Bank for International Settlements, Consumer prices (WS_LONG_CPI); OECD, Consumer price indices (DSD_PRICES@DF_PRICES_ALL), core CPI, on the OECD Data Explorer; Eurostat, HICP monthly data, annual rate of change (prc_hicp_minr), euro-area core; recession bands: NBER-based Recession Indicators for the United States (USREC), via FRED, from the dates of the NBER Business Cycle Dating Committee. Prepared files: data/ch12/fig12-15.csv, data/ch12/cpi_monthly.csv, data/ch12/recessions.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 12.15 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

What to notice.

  • At the start of the pandemic, inflation fell, as the Phillips curve predicts for a weak economy: from 2.6 percent in January 2020 to 0.2 percent in May 2020.
  • Within a year it rose to levels not seen in four decades: 9.0 percent in June 2022 (the last higher reading was 9.6 percent in November 1981). Core inflation peaked later, at 6.6 percent in September 2022.
  • Inflation then came down, without a recession, to between 2.3 and 3.0 percent from mid-2024 through 2025. From March 2026 headline inflation rose back above 3 percent (4.2 percent in May) while core inflation stayed near 2.5 percent, a sign of a new price shock (\(\bar{o} > 0\)).
  • Choose the euro area or the United Kingdom: inflation peaked later and higher than in the United States, at 10.6 and 11.1 percent in October 2022, pushed up by energy prices after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Their core inflation peaked only in 2023 (5.7 percent in March and 6.5 percent in May).

Your turn. In which month did all-items inflation first fall below 3 percent after its 2022 peak?

Keep the rows after the peak with cpi.date > "2022-06-01" and cpi.inflation_all < 3, then take the first date.

What to notice.

Government spending in other countries

Federal outlays are a U.S. concept. To compare countries we need general government spending: all levels of government together (in the United States, federal, state and local), by calendar year. The IMF’s Fiscal Monitor publishes it for 194 economies. For the United States it is 13 to 17 points of GDP higher than the federal share, but it moved the same way: up 8.9 points from 2019 to 2020, against 9.8 points for federal outlays.

Python note. part.set_index("year").spending_gdp labels the values by year, so .get(2019) picks the value of 2019, or gives None when the year is missing.

def spending_chart(countries=("United States",)):
    """Fig. 12.16, extended: general government spending, percent of GDP, in the chosen countries."""
    part = spending[spending.country.isin(countries) & (spending.year >= 2007)]
    high = 70
    if part.spending_gdp.max() > high:              # a few small islands spend more than their GDP
        high = 140
    title = "General government spending, percent of GDP"
    by_year = part.set_index("year").spending_gdp
    if len(countries) == 1 and by_year.get(2019) is not None and by_year.get(2020) is not None:
        title = f"{countries[0]}: spending went from {by_year[2019]:.1f}% of GDP in 2019 to {by_year[2020]:.1f}% in 2020"
    title += missing_or_off(part, "spending_gdp", countries, 0, high)
    fig = px.line(part, x="year", y="spending_gdp", color="country", color_discrete_map=SPENDING_COLORS, markers=True,
                  labels={"year": "Year", "spending_gdp": "Percent of GDP", "country": "Country"}, title=title)
    fig.update_traces(line_width=3, marker_size=7)
    fig.update_layout(xaxis_range=[2006.5, 2025.5], yaxis_range=[0, high], legend_title_text="")
    return fig

def household_chart(country="United States"):
    """Fig. 12.17, extended: real household income and consumption per person, 2019Q4 = 100."""
    part = households[households.country == country].rename(
        columns={"income_pc": "Disposable income per person", "consumption_pc": "Consumption per person"})
    values = part[["Disposable income per person", "Consumption per person"]]
    for low, high in [(80, 120), (70, 130), (60, 170)]:
        if values.min().min() >= low and values.max().max() <= high:
            break                                       # the first range that holds every value
    by_date = part.set_index("date")
    income = round(by_date["Disposable income per person"].get(pd.Timestamp("2021-01-01"), np.nan) - 100, 1)
    spent = round(by_date["Consumption per person"].get(pd.Timestamp("2021-01-01"), np.nan) - 100, 1)
    title = f"{country}, 2021Q1 vs 2019Q4: real income per person {income + 0.0:+.1f}%, consumption {spent + 0.0:+.1f}%"
    if np.isnan(income):
        title = f"{country}, 2021Q1 vs 2019Q4: consumption per person {spent + 0.0:+.1f}% (no income data)"
    fig = px.line(part, x="date", y=list(values.columns), markers=True, color_discrete_sequence=[BLUE, TEAL], title=title,
                  labels={"date": "Year", "value": "Index, 2019Q4 = 100", "variable": "Series"})
    fig.add_hline(y=100, line_dash="dot", line_color=GRAY)
    fig.update_layout(xaxis_range=["2016-10-01", "2026-04-01"], yaxis_range=[low, high], legend_title_text=country,
                      legend=dict(x=0.01, y=0.99, xanchor="left", yanchor="top"))
    return fig

# Your turn: try it here

How central banks control the nominal interest rate

So far the central bank simply chose the interest rate. The money market shows how it does so: by supplying whatever money is demanded at its target rate.

Fig. 18: How the central bank sets the nominal interest rate

Goal. See where “money” comes in: the central bank sets the interest rate through the money market.

The nominal interest rate is the opportunity cost of holding money: cash and checking accounts pay nothing, while a savings or money-market account pays \(i\). At 1 percent you might as well hold cash; at 20 percent you would keep as little as possible. So money demand \(M^d\) falls as \(i\) rises. The central bank decides how much money to supply, \(M^s\): a vertical line. The interest rate \(i^*\) is where people want to hold exactly the money supplied. If \(i\) were higher, people would want less money than there is, and the rate would fall; if lower, the opposite.

As before, one function draws two textbook figures: this one (12.18) and a change in the money supply (12.19). Its arguments are the new money supply M_new and the new level of money demand m0_new (demand is \(M^d = m_0 - i\)).

Python note. "Mᵈ′" if m0_new != M0 else "Mᵈ" is a one-line if: it gives the first text when the condition is true and the second otherwise.

def money_experiment(M_new=M_BAR, m0_new=M0):
    """Figs. 12.18 and 12.19: money supply and demand set the nominal rate; a change moves i* to i**."""
    i_star, i_new = market_rate(M_BAR), market_rate(M_new, m0_new)
    fig = go.Figure()
    if m0_new != M0:
        add_demand(fig, "Mᵈ", GRAY, M0, "dash")
    add_demand(fig, "Mᵈ′" if m0_new != M0 else "Mᵈ", BLUE, m0_new)
    if M_new != M_BAR:
        add_line(fig, [M_BAR, M_BAR], [0.5, 9.5], "Mˢ", GRAY, "dash")
        add_arrow(fig, M_BAR, 1.0, M_new, 1.0)                     # the change in the money supply
    add_line(fig, [M_new, M_new], [0.5, 9.5], "Mˢ′" if M_new != M_BAR else "Mˢ", TEAL)
    where = "bottom left" if m0_new > M0 else "top right"      # keep i* clear of a higher demand curve
    add_point(fig, M_BAR, i_star, "i*", 0, 0, where=where)
    if i_new != i_star:
        where = "bottom left" if m0_new < M0 else "top right"  # ... and i** clear of the old, higher one
        add_point(fig, M_new, i_new, "i**", 0, 0, where=where)
        add_arrow(fig, 0.5, i_star, 0.5, i_new)                    # the change in the interest rate
    set_axes(fig, X_MONEY, Y_NOMINAL)
    fig.update_layout(title=f"Money supply {M_new:.1f}, demand Mᵈ = {m0_new:.1f} − i  →  i = {i_star:.1f}% → {i_new:.1f}%",
                      margin=dict(r=90))
    return fig
interact(money_experiment,
         M_new=FloatSlider(value=5.0, min=3.5, max=7.0, step=0.5, description="money supply Mˢ", style=WIDE),
         m0_new=FloatSlider(value=10.0, min=8.0, max=12.0, step=0.5, description="money demand at i = 0, m₀", style=WIDE));
Show the code of the website version 
# @title Website version: Fig. 18 with a precomputed slider for money demand
slider_figure(money_experiment, "m0_new", [8.0, 9.0, 10.0, 11.0, 12.0], start=10.0, label="money demand at i = 0, m₀")

Source. Adapted from Fig. 12.18 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

What to notice.

  • With a supply of 5 and demand \(M^d = 10 - i\), the market clears at \(i^* = 5\) percent.
  • Move money demand: with the money supply fixed, every shift of demand moves the interest rate one for one. People need more money when prices or output are higher, or less when they pay by card, so demand shifts all the time.
  • In the short run inflation is sticky, so the money market clears through the interest rate (and the velocity of money), not through the price level as in the quantity theory of Chapter 8.

Your turn. Money demand rises to \(M^d = 11 - i\) because people make more purchases. What money supply keeps the interest rate at 5 percent? Check it with market_rate.

Hint

You need \(11 - i = M^s\) at \(i = 5\). Then try market_rate(6.0, m0=11.0).

# Your turn: try it here

Fig. 19: Raising the nominal interest rate

Goal. See what “tight money” means: to raise the interest rate, the central bank reduces the money supply.

The money supply shifts left, from \(M^s\) to \(M^{s\prime}\). At the old rate \(i^*\), people now want more money than there is: households ask their banks for cash, and banks must offer a higher interest rate on savings accounts to bring money demand back in line with supply. The rate rises to \(i^{**}\). We use our illustrative cut from 5 to 4 units of money.

interact(money_experiment,
         M_new=FloatSlider(value=4.0, min=3.5, max=7.0, step=0.5, description="new money supply Mˢ′", style=WIDE),
         m0_new=FloatSlider(value=10.0, min=8.0, max=12.0, step=0.5, description="money demand at i = 0, m₀", style=WIDE));
Show the code of the website version 
# @title Website version: Fig. 19 with a precomputed slider for the new money supply
slider_figure(money_experiment, "M_new", [3.5, 4.0, 4.5, 5.0, 5.5, 6.0, 6.5, 7.0], start=4.0, label="new money supply Mˢ′")

Source. Adapted from Fig. 12.19 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

What to notice.

  • Cutting the money supply from 5 to 4 raises the nominal rate from 5 to 6 percent: tight money means a higher interest rate.
  • A larger money supply (“loose” money) lowers the rate: move the slider to the right.
  • In practice the Fed changes the money supply by open-market operations: it sells government bonds to take money out of the economy, or buys them to put money in (see the key numbers in Fig. 20).

Your turn. The Fed wants to cut the nominal rate from 5 to 4.5 percent. By how much must it increase the money supply?

Hint

With demand \(10 - i\), the supply must equal \(10 - 4.5\). Check with market_rate(5.5).

# Your turn: try it here

Fig. 20: Targeting the nominal interest rate

Goal. See why central banks set an interest rate rather than a quantity of money.

Money demand shifts all the time (Fig. 18). If the central bank kept the money supply fixed, every shift would move the interest rate, and with it the real rate and output. Instead, modern central banks peg the interest rate: they supply whatever money is demanded at the target rate \(i^*\). The money supply curve becomes horizontal at \(i^*\), and shifts in money demand change the quantity of money, not the rate. Compare the two policies with the toggle.

Python note. ToggleButtons shows one button per option, and the function receives the text of the chosen button.

def rate_target(m0_new=M0, i_target=5.0, policy="peg the interest rate"):
    """Fig. 12.20: pegging i makes money supply horizontal; fixing M lets money-demand shocks move i."""
    fig = go.Figure()
    if m0_new != M0:
        add_demand(fig, "Mᵈ", GRAY, M0, "dash")
    add_demand(fig, "Mᵈ′" if m0_new != M0 else "Mᵈ", BLUE, m0_new)
    if policy == "peg the interest rate":
        i_eq, M_eq = i_target, money_demand(i_target, m0_new)
        add_line(fig, [0.5, 10.5], [i_target, i_target], "Mˢ", TEAL)
    else:
        M_eq = money_demand(i_target)                  # the supply that gave i_target before the shock
        i_eq = market_rate(M_eq, m0_new)
        add_line(fig, [M_eq, M_eq], [0.5, 9.5], "Mˢ", TEAL)
    add_point(fig, M_eq, i_eq, "", 0, 0)
    set_axes(fig, X_MONEY, Y_NOMINAL)
    fig.update_layout(title=f"Policy: {policy};  demand shift {m0_new - M0:+.1f}  →  i = {i_eq:.1f}%, M = {M_eq:.1f}",
                      margin=dict(r=90))
    return fig
interact(rate_target,
         m0_new=FloatSlider(value=11.0, min=8.0, max=12.0, step=0.5, description="money demand at i = 0, m₀", style=WIDE),
         i_target=FloatSlider(value=5.0, min=3.0, max=7.0, step=0.5, description="target rate i* (%)", style=WIDE),
         policy=ToggleButtons(options=["peg the interest rate", "fix the money supply"], value="peg the interest rate",
                              description="policy", style=WIDE));
Show the code of the website version 
# @title Website version: Fig. 20 with a precomputed slider for money demand (the rate is pegged)
slider_figure(rate_target, "m0_new", [8.0, 9.0, 10.0, 11.0, 12.0], start=11.0, label="money demand at i = 0, m₀")

Source. Adapted from Fig. 12.20 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

What to notice.

  • With the rate pegged at 5 percent, a rise in money demand from \(m_0 = 10\) to 11 is met by more money (6 instead of 5), and the interest rate does not move.
  • Switch to “fix the money supply”: the same shift raises the interest rate to 6 percent, which would push the real rate up and output down although nothing real happened. Pegging the rate shields the economy from money-demand shocks.
  • The IS/LM model. An older version of the short-run model keeps the money supply fixed. Then higher output raises money demand and the interest rate, which gives an upward-sloping “LM” curve instead of our flat MP curve. Since central banks in fact adjust the money supply to keep the interest rate at its target, the two approaches lead to the same analysis.

Key numbers: bond prices and interest rates

In an open-market operation the Fed buys or sells bonds, and the interest rate is hidden in the bond’s price. A bond that pays 100 dollars in one year and sells for 97 dollars today yields \(3/97 = 3.1\) percent.

def bond_yield(price, face=100.0):
    """The one-year interest rate implied by a bond's price: (face - price) / price, in percent."""
    return 100 * (face - price) / price


for price in [95.0, 96.0, 97.0, 98.0, 99.0]:
    print(f"Price {price:.0f}  ->  yield {bond_yield(price):.2f}%")
Price 95  ->  yield 5.26%
Price 96  ->  yield 4.17%
Price 97  ->  yield 3.09%
Price 98  ->  yield 2.04%
Price 99  ->  yield 1.01%

When the Fed sells bonds, their price falls and the interest rate rises (tight money); when it buys bonds, their price rises and the rate falls.

Your turn. At what price would a one-year bond with a face value of 100 dollars yield 5 percent?

Hint

Solve \((100 - P)/P = 0.05\), so \(P = 100/1.05\). Check it with bond_yield(100 / 1.05).

Worked exercise: the Great Inflation

The last figure is the textbook’s answer to Exercise 12: what happens when policymakers mistake a slowdown in potential output for a demand shock and keep stimulating.

Fig. 21: The Great Inflation

Goal. Answer Exercise 12 of the textbook: how mistaking the productivity slowdown for a demand shock could have caused the Great Inflation.

The four panels tell the story of Fig. 13 with the model’s diagrams:

    1. Policymakers believe a negative demand shock \(\bar{a}' < 0\) caused the slowdown: they think the IS curve shifted to IS′, and the economy is at \(B\), below potential.
    1. So they lower the real interest rate to \(R' = \bar{r} + \bar{a}'/\bar{b}\), which, they believe, takes the economy back to potential at \(C\).
    1. Demand never actually fell, so the IS curve is where it was. The lower rate moves the economy down the true IS curve, to \(C\), above potential.
    1. With output above potential, the Phillips curve raises inflation: \(\downarrow R \Rightarrow \uparrow \tilde{Y} \Rightarrow \uparrow \pi\).

The figure has four panels, so we split the work: perceived_panels draws the two panels of what policymakers believe, and great_inflation adds the truth and the readout.

def perceived_panels(fig, a_perc, R_new):
    """Fig. 12.21 (a) and (b): the IS/MP diagram as policymakers see it."""
    for col in [1, 2]:
        add_is(fig, "IS", GRAY, dash="dash", row=1, col=col)
        add_is(fig, "IS′", TEAL, a_perc, row=1, col=col)
        add_point(fig, 0.0, R_BAR, "A", -8, 0, 1, col)
        add_point(fig, a_perc, R_BAR, "B", -8, 0, 1, col)
        set_axes(fig, X_OUTPUT, Y_RATE, 1, col)
    add_line(fig, MP_X, [R_BAR, R_BAR], "MP", BLUE, row=1, col=1)
    add_arrow(fig, 0.0, 0.6, a_perc, 0.6, 1, 1)
    add_line(fig, MP_X, [R_BAR, R_BAR], "MP", GRAY, "dash", 1, 2)
    add_line(fig, MP_X, [R_new, R_new], "MP′", BLUE, row=1, col=2)
    add_point(fig, 0.0, R_new, "C", -8, 0, 1, 2, where="bottom left")    # below left, clear of A
    add_arrow(fig, a_perc, 0.6, 0.0, 0.6, 1, 2)
def great_inflation(a_perc=-2.0, nu=NU):
    """Fig. 12.21: the Fed sees a demand shock a' that never happened, cuts R, and inflation rises."""
    R_new = rate_for_output(0.0, a_perc)           # the cut that would close the perceived gap
    Y_true = is_curve(R_new)                       # but the true IS curve never moved
    dpi = phillips(Y_true, nu)
    fig = make_subplots(rows=2, cols=2, horizontal_spacing=0.12, vertical_spacing=0.14,
                        subplot_titles=("(a) Belief: demand fell, IS → IS′", "(b) Belief: a cut to R′ restores Ỹ = 0",
                                        "(c) Reality: IS unchanged, Ỹ overshoots", "(d) Reality: Ỹ > 0 pushes Δπ up"))
    perceived_panels(fig, a_perc, R_new)
    add_is(fig, "IS", TEAL, row=2, col=1)
    add_line(fig, MP_X, [R_BAR, R_BAR], "MP", GRAY, "dash", 2, 1)
    add_line(fig, MP_X, [R_new, R_new], "MP′", BLUE, row=2, col=1)
    add_point(fig, 0.0, R_BAR, "A", -8, 0, 2, 1)
    add_point(fig, Y_true, R_new, "C", -8, 0, 2, 1, where="bottom left")  # clear of the old MP line
    add_arrow(fig, 0.0, 0.6, Y_true, 0.6, 2, 1)
    add_pc(fig, "Phillips curve", GREEN, nu, row=2, col=2)
    add_point(fig, 0.0, 0.0, "A", -8, -4, 2, 2, where="top left")
    add_point(fig, Y_true, dpi, "B", -8, -4, 2, 2, where="top left")
    set_axes(fig, X_OUTPUT, Y_RATE, 2, 1)
    set_axes(fig, X_OUTPUT, Y_DPI, 2, 2)
    fig.update_layout(height=820, title=f"Believed ā′ = {a_perc:.1f}  →  R′ = {R_new:.2f}%  →  true Ỹ = {Y_true:+.1f}%"
                                        f"  →  Δπ = {dpi:+.2f} a year")
    return fig
interact(great_inflation,
         a_perc=FloatSlider(value=-2.0, min=-3.0, max=-0.5, step=0.5, description="demand shock policymakers believe in ā′", style=WIDE),
         nu=FloatSlider(value=0.5, min=0.25, max=1.0, step=0.05, description="slope ν̄", style=WIDE));
Show the code of the website version 
# @title Website version: Fig. 21 with a precomputed slider for the believed demand shock
slider_figure(great_inflation, "a_perc", [-3.0, -2.5, -2.0, -1.5], start=-2.0,
              label="demand shock policymakers believe in ā′")

Source. Adapted from Fig. 12.21 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed., the worked answer to Exercise 12.

What to notice.

  • Believing in a shock of \(-2\), the Fed cuts \(R\) from 5 to 4 percent. On the true IS curve this takes output to \(+2\) percent, not 0, and inflation rises by 1 point a year for as long as the mistake lasts.
  • The bigger the shock policymakers believe in, the bigger the cut, the bigger the boom, and the faster inflation rises.
  • How can policymakers find out? Rising inflation with no other shock is the sign that output is above potential. In the 1970s the oil shocks also raised inflation, so the mistake took years to see.

Your turn. Suppose the Fed recognizes its mistake and wants to stop inflation from rising. To what real interest rate should it return? What if, in addition, it wants to bring inflation back down by 1 point a year?

Hint

Steady inflation needs \(\tilde{Y} = 0\) on the true IS curve: rate_for_output(0.0). Lowering inflation by 1 point a year needs \(\tilde{Y} = -1/\bar{\nu}\): try rate_for_output(-2.0).

# Your turn: try it here

Concluding remarks

  • The short-run model has three building blocks. Through the MP curve, the central bank’s nominal interest rate sets the real interest rate, because inflation is sticky. Through the IS curve, the real rate sets short-run output. Through the Phillips curve, \(\Delta\pi_t = \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t + \bar{o}\), output changes inflation over time.
  • In the IS/MP diagram, monetary policy can in principle offset demand shocks such as a housing bust, but long and variable lags make this hard in practice.
  • Lowering inflation requires a temporary recession: the Volcker disinflation brought inflation from 13.5 percent in 1980 to 3.2 percent in 1983, at the cost of the deepest recession in decades. Oil shocks, the belief in a permanent trade-off, and a productivity slowdown mistaken for a recession all contributed to the Great Inflation of the 1970s.
  • Central banks set the interest rate by supplying whatever money is demanded at their target. Through the term structure, the short rate also moves longer-term rates.
  • The next chapter adds the central bank’s policy rule and expectations, leading to the AS/AD framework.
